title: New Details Emerge in Amazon Ads Auction-Rigging Case
text: The Federal Trade Commission and 22 states recently filed an updated version of their complaint against Amazon with unredacted details about Amazon’s alleged use of deceptive and unfair practices to secretly inflate prices in its online search advertising auction. Details in the updated version of the complaint show substantial harm to advertisers as well as the direct statements Amazon made to mislead advertisers about the true cause of the price increases resulting from its scheme. In August, the FTC and its state partners sued Amazon in the Western District of Washington, arguing that the online retailer harmed advertisers by covertly and substantially increasing the prices charged to them for advertising on Amazon’s platforms. The new filing makes public factual details that had previously been redacted. The unredacted portions of the complaint allege that Amazon secretly raises advertising prices by as much as 50% above auction results on ordinary days and by as much as 250% on major shopping days like Prime Day or Black Friday. Amazon’s efforts led to significantly higher advertising prices during high-volume shopping days. Newly unsealed portions of the complaint allege that during the 2021 holiday season, Amazon increased advertisers’ average cost-per-click by 20%, with some advertisers experiencing increases of over 200%. Similarly, during the 2022 holiday shopping season, Amazon secretly and successfully raised its surcharges to increase its revenue by $87 million worldwide. Neither small businesses nor large and sophisticated customers were spared from the surcharges. One large food and beverage advertiser, for example, was subjected to price increases of more than 100% during Prime Day in 2023. Internally, Amazon acknowledged that its price increases led to decreases in the advertiser’s return on ad spend that were “destroying campaign performance.” The unsealed allegations also demonstrate that Amazon used its hidden surcharges to meet revenue goals. In 2023, Amazon executives discussed the need to find an additional $40 million in revenue to meet corporate financial targets, according to the complaint. Per the complaint, the head of Amazon Ads told Amazon’s senior vice president of ad products and technology in an email that, “I’d like to pull out all of the stops (without doing unnatural acts) to close our gaps to plan. I suspect that the entire gap won’t be closed, so whatever can be done with reserves (ideally at least $40MM would be helpful).” As alleged in the unredacted portions of the complaint, when advertisers facing prices inflated by Amazon’s hidden surcharges asked if “something has changed with respect to the second price auction process,” Amazon falsely reassured them the price increases were the result of increased competition. In one instance, for example, after being directly asked by an advertiser whether “something has changed with respect to the second price auction process, either by design or mistake,” an Amazon account manager falsely stated, “After reaching out to the product specialist team we were informed there is not a bug, or a change in auction style, so no worries there. This year the marketplace is even more crowded than any year previous, and we are seeing the spike in CPCs [costs-per-click] as a direct reflection.” The attorneys general of Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Vermont and Washington joined in filing the now-unredacted complaint.

title: Statement of the Department of Justice Antitrust Division on the Closing of Its Investigation of the Merger of FOX and Roku
text: The U.S. Department of Justice issued the following statement today in connection with the closing of the Antitrust Division’s investigation into the proposed acquisition of Roku Inc. (Roku) by FOX Corporation (FOX) (together, the “Parties”). On June 15, FOX announced its intent to acquire Roku for approximately $22 billion. FOX operates several media companies, including FOX News Media, FOX Entertainment, FOX Television Stations, and Tubi, a free, ad-supported streaming service. Roku sells connected TV devices, televisions, streaming players, and smart home devices and operates a connected TV platform that users can use to access hundreds of streaming applications. Roku also owns and operates a free, ad-supported streaming service, The Roku Channel (TRC). The Division opened an investigation and issued second requests to FOX and Roku. The Division analyzed whether the proposed merger may harm competition among free, ad-supported streaming providers. The Division also considered whether FOX might use its control of the Roku platform to disadvantage its content rivals post-merger. The Division concluded that the entry of free, ad-supported streaming providers would be timely, likely, and sufficient to make a substantial risk of harm to competition unlikely. Additionally, the investigation found that, because Roku relies on a broad offering of content from many providers to attract consumers, the merged firm would suffer monetary and reputational harm if it attempted to use the Roku platform to harm FOX’s content rivals. If the merged firm were to degrade the Roku platform, consumers could switch to other connected TV platforms. Given the facts surrounding the investigation, the Division anticipates that the transaction is not likely to result in harm to competition. Consistent with the Division’s finding that the transaction is unlikely to result in harm to competition, FOX has committed that Roku will remain an open and neutral content partner post-merger. More specifically, FOX has committed to the following: FOX will continue carrying non-FOX content on Roku for a period of at least 3 years consistent with historical Roku practice. FOX will not discriminate against non-FOX content in search results. For application placement on Roku, FOX will continue to allow users to reconfigure application configurations on the home screen. FOX will continue to provide data products to third parties on commercially reasonable terms consistent with Roku’s standard distribution agreement. FOX will maintain existing contractual firewall commitments to content partners for competitively sensitive non-FOX content data, including aggregated and non-aggregated data that can be inferred from, or collected through, commercial activities of non-FOX content providers or their uses on Roku products, including click, search, view, and voice data for a period of at least 3 years. Following this review, the Division decided that its investigation could be closed. The Division will continue to evaluate competition in the industry and may take appropriate action in light of changing facts or circumstances.

title: Former Army Official Pleads Guilty to Conspiracy, Bribery, and Major Fraud Related to Hawaii Defense Contracts
text: A former civilian U.S. Army official pleaded guilty today to participating in a bribery and major fraud scheme that corrupted the competitive process for a U.S. Army technology innovation lab in the Pacific. According to a plea agreement and information filed in the U.S. District Court in Honolulu, Hawaii, from January 2021 to October 2022, Carlos Duque conspired with two defense contractors — Brian Kent and Leonard Pick — to accept a bribe of approximately $1.25 million over five years. In return, Duque told prime contractors to award subcontracts to Kent and Pick’s company and facilitated their fraudulent inflation of government contracting costs to include Duque’s bribe payments. Duque ultimately received approximately $55,000 in bribes from his coconspirators and the United States Army paid over $3 million to Kent and Pick’s company. “Fraud that deprives the U.S. military of free and fair competition for government contracts harms us all,” said Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. “Because of prosecutions like this, Americans can trust that the Department of War and its warfighters maintain the highest standards of integrity. We expect their contractors to do the same.” “Those who commit fraud on defense contracts don’t just steal from the military or taxpayers; they threaten the public’s confidence in government institutions and hurt our military readiness,” said Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General Daniel W. Glad of the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division. “The Justice Department’s Procurement Collusion Strike Force will detect and prosecute those who, like the defendant, attempt to illegally take advantage of government programs.” “Americans work hard for their money and have every right to expect that their tax dollars will not be diverted through fraudulent schemes,” said U.S. Attorney Ken Sorenson for the District of Hawaii. “Those who obtain military contracts through fraud undermine both the public trust and the mission of our armed forces, and they will be held accountable.” “Public corruption — especially when it compromises our nation’s military readiness — undermines trust in the institutions built to protect our country,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Ryan C. Noonan of the FBI Honolulu Field Office. “This guilty plea reflects the strength of our partnerships in safeguarding government resources and ensuring integrity in the procurement process. Together with our federal law enforcement and military investigative partners, the FBI remains committed to identifying and stopping schemes that undermine fair competition and betray the public’s trust.” “Public officials are entrusted with a duty to the American people and government service is not an opportunity for personal enrichment at taxpayer expense,” said Director James R. Ives of the Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS), the criminal investigative arm of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General. “DCIS and our partners remain steadfast in aggressively investigating those who undermine fair and open competition in government contracting.” “U.S. Army employees and defense contractors are trusted to comply with the law and maintain the highest ethical standards,” said Special Agent in Charge Michael DeFamio, Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division Asia Pacific Field Office. “This conspiracy to trade subcontracts for over a million dollars in kickbacks is a direct betrayal of their promise to support our nation. Army CID, alongside the Department of Justice and our federal law enforcement partners, is committed to finding corrupt employees and defense contractors who would compromise the resources, safety, and trust of our men and women in uniform.” “Bribery corrupts the federal contracting process that supports the critical missions of our military and civilian agencies,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Ryan Gregg of U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) Office of Inspector General (OIG) Western Investigations Division. “GSA OIG special agents will continue to aggressively pursue fraud alongside our law enforcement partners and the Department of Justice.” “By exploiting a position of public trust to advance private interests, Mr. Duque undermined the integrity of the Department of the Navy’s competitive procurement process,” said Special Agent in Charge Brian Merkal of the NCIS Economic Crimes Field Office. “NCIS and our law enforcement partners remain committed to investigating and pursuing accountability for those who abuse American taxpayer trust by manipulating fair and impartial DON programs for personal gain.” Duque pleaded guilty to conspiracy, bribery, and major fraud. Under the conspiracy charge, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000. Under the bribery charge, Duque faces a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison, a fine of up to $250,000 or not more than three times the monetary equivalent of the bribe, whichever is greater, and disqualification from holding any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States. Under the major fraud charge, Duque faces a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $5,000,000. In addition, Duque agreed to forfeit $55,166.70 as part of the plea agreement. title: NIST Report Provides Guidelines for Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
text: NEWS NIST Report Provides Guidelines for Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards October 27, 2026 Share Facebook Linkedin X.com Email A finalized report will help organizations transition to NIST’s post-quantum standards, which are necessary to withstand attacks by future quantum computers. The report identifies existing quantum-vulnerable cryptographic standards and the quantum-resistant standards that are designed to replace them. This report describes the timelines and migration activities for federal agencies, and it can serve as a key resource for technology providers and organizations that are developing their quantum-readiness road maps. Credit: J. Wang/NIST and Shutterstock In August 2024, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards made to withstand the assault of a future quantum computer. Now, the agency has released its high-level road map to help organizations switch to these standards. The report, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (NISTIR 8547) , outlines NIST’s official approach and timelines for transitioning away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms to quantum-resistant standards. It is the core technical document meant to inform federal agencies, industry partners and standards organizations about what needs to change and when during the migration to PQC standards — a cryptographic modernization with details that will vary by organization but timelines that apply broadly. “The report describes different use cases and says why one migration might take longer than another,” said NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who heads the PQC standardization project. “We understand there’s not one strategy that fits all use cases, and we want to help people handle their migration while staying abreast of what’s changing.” While quantum computers are still in development, a sufficiently powerful device — known as a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer — would threaten the encryption methods that protect our confidential electronic information, from email messages to financial statements. Even though the transition to PQC is beginning before such a device appears, today’s encrypted data is already at risk from the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat, where adversaries collect sensitive data now with the intention of decrypting it when quantum technology matures. This threat is one of the main reasons why the transition to PQC is urgent, driving the need to make changes on a well-considered schedule. National Security Memorandum 10 established the year 2035 as the primary target for completing the migration to PQC across federal systems. Executive Order 14412 accelerated this timeline, requiring federal high-value assets and high-impact systems to migrate by 2030 for key establishment and 2031 for digital signatures. NISTIR 8547 supports these migration timelines. While the memorandum applies specifically to federal systems, many organizations that work with the federal government will be affected as well. The NIST report identifies quantum-vulnerable algorithms among NIST’s existing cryptographic standards. The report then provides the transition plan for the quantum-vulnerable algorithms in these standards, referencing the post-quantum algorithm standards NIST published in 2024. “We lay out how certain encryption algorithms people are using today will get phased out,” Moody said. “It’s important to know how a given algorithm might be disallowed in federal systems after a certain date, for instance, or whether it will be allowed but at the user’s own risk. Factors like this can help an organization plan.” Because migration is a logistically complex undertaking, the report also helps delineate the numerous factors that organizations should consider to complete the process. Not only are an organization’s own system components important, but also its entire cryptographic supply chain. Some actions may take priority over others, Moody said. For example, because of the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat, organizations might prioritize migrating to the PQC key establishment standard ( FIPS 203 ) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to be kept secure for a long time. The report also discusses the option of taking a hybrid approach, in which an organization hedges its bets by combining conventional encryption with PQC, akin to using two padlocks on a door instead of one. NIST accommodates this option, which has the advantage of being more conservative from a security standpoint but also demands more computational resources. The publication’s contents complement the migration to PQC guidelines project at NIST’s National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE). The project has established a cross-sector collaboration focused on the use of the NIST PQC standards — working on demonstrations of cryptographic visibility and risk management practices to prioritize migration to PQC. The project aims to highlight considerations of cryptographic agility and demonstrations of PQC implementations to support migration timelines. “The new report can help you understand the standards and requirements of the migration,” Moody said, “while the NCCoE project can show you the practical tools and blueprints to get the job done.” Information technology , Cybersecurity and privacy and Cryptography Media Contact Chad Boutin [email protected] (301) 975-4261 NIST in your inbox Learn More NIST IR 8547: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards NIST Releases First 3 Finalized Post-Quantum Encryption Standards PQC Standardization Process Organizations NIST Headquarters Laboratory Programs Information Technology Laboratory Computer Security Division Cryptographic Technology Group Released October 27, 2026, Updated November 2, 2026

  • A finalized report will help organizations transition to NIST’s post-quantum standards, which are necessary to withstand attacks by future quantum computers.
  • The report identifies existing quantum-vulnerable cryptographic standards and the quantum-resistant standards that are designed to replace them.
  • This report describes the timelines and migration activities for federal agencies, and it can serve as a key resource for technology providers and organizations that are developing their quantum-readiness road maps.

In August 2024, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards made to withstand the assault of a future quantum computer. Now, the agency has released its high-level road map to help organizations switch to these standards. 

The report, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (NISTIR 8547), outlines NIST’s official approach and timelines for transitioning away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms to quantum-resistant standards. It is the core technical document meant to inform federal agencies, industry partners and standards organizations about what needs to change and when during the migration to PQC standards — a cryptographic modernization with details that will vary by organization but timelines that apply broadly.

“The report describes different use cases and says why one migration might take longer than another,” said NIST mathematician Dustin Moody, who heads the PQC standardization project. “We understand there’s not one strategy that fits all use cases, and we want to help people handle their migration while staying abreast of what’s changing.”

While quantum computers are still in development, a sufficiently powerful device — known as a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer — would threaten the encryption methods that protect our confidential electronic information, from email messages to financial statements. Even though the transition to PQC is beginning before such a device appears, today’s encrypted data is already at risk from the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat, where adversaries collect sensitive data now with the intention of decrypting it when quantum technology matures. This threat is one of the main reasons why the transition to PQC is urgent, driving the need to make changes on a well-considered schedule.

National Security Memorandum 10 established the year 2035 as the primary target for completing the migration to PQC across federal systems. Executive Order 14412 accelerated this timeline, requiring federal high-value assets and high-impact systems to migrate by 2030 for key establishment and 2031 for digital signatures. NISTIR 8547 supports these migration timelines. While the memorandum applies specifically to federal systems, many organizations that work with the federal government will be affected as well. 

The NIST report identifies quantum-vulnerable algorithms among NIST’s existing cryptographic standards. The report then provides the transition plan for the quantum-vulnerable algorithms in these standards, referencing the post-quantum algorithm standards NIST published in 2024.

“We lay out how certain encryption algorithms people are using today will get phased out,” Moody said. “It’s important to know how a given algorithm might be disallowed in federal systems after a certain date, for instance, or whether it will be allowed but at the user’s own risk. Factors like this can help an organization plan.”

Because migration is a logistically complex undertaking, the report also helps delineate the numerous factors that organizations should consider to complete the process. Not only are an organization’s own system components important, but also its entire cryptographic supply chain. 

Some actions may take priority over others, Moody said. For example, because of the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat, organizations might prioritize migrating to the PQC key establishment standard (FIPS 203) for data that is particularly sensitive or needs to be kept secure for a long time.

The report also discusses the option of taking a hybrid approach, in which an organization hedges its bets by combining conventional encryption with PQC, akin to using two padlocks on a door instead of one. NIST accommodates this option, which has the advantage of being more conservative from a security standpoint but also demands more computational resources. 

The publication’s contents complement the migration to PQC guidelines project at NIST’s National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE). The project has established a cross-sector collaboration focused on the use of the NIST PQC standards — working on demonstrations of cryptographic visibility and risk management practices to prioritize migration to PQC. The project aims to highlight considerations of cryptographic agility and demonstrations of PQC implementations to support migration timelines.

“The new report can help you understand the standards and requirements of the migration,” Moody said, “while the NCCoE project can show you the practical tools and blueprints to get the job done.”

title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
text: The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies. The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying. Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system. In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only 37 IPR petitions were filed in September 2026, compared to 129 petitions in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges. This dramatic decline shouldn’t just concern patent lawyers. EFF has fought bad patents because so many software and internet patents make claims to the basic tools of free expression online, like sending email, using online ads, or publishing web pages. When bad patents go unchallenged, they affect everyone who cares about the freedom to write new code and make new technology. That’s why EFF has defended IPR since it came on the scene more than a decade ago. It provides a faster and less expensive way to challenge patents that should never have been granted. Congress created IPRs because the Patent Office makes mistakes. District court litigation is an extraordinarily expensive way to correct them. Without a meaningful administrative review process, bad patents remain powerful weapons in the hands of patent trolls and others seeking to extract settlements from companies that often did nothing wrong. Now, USPTO leadership is dismantling that safeguard. Petitions and Institution Rates Are Falling Since Congress created the IPR patent challenge process in 2012, the PTAB has always had some discretion in deciding which petitions deserve review. But institution rates today are much lower than their typical historical range. Between fiscal years 2022 and 2024, the PTAB instituted between 66% and 68% of IPR petitions . In fiscal year 2026, which concluded in September 2026, the institution rate fell to 41% . And institution is only the first step of an IPR—it means the PTAB has agreed to hear the challenge, not that the challenger won, and the patent will be invalidated. That decline helps explain why fewer petitions are being filed in the first place. Preparing an IPR petition takes substantial time and money. While cheaper than federal court, it’s still a complicated administrative process. Before filing, a challenger typically needs to search for prior art, hire experts, and develop detailed technical and legal arguments about why the patent never should have been granted. Companies were willing to pay for IPRs because, historically, they could expect a predictable process. Petitions that met the statutory standard generally had a reasonable prospect of being heard and decided on the merits. But the USPTO has made it harder to get petitions heard and is throwing them out for reasons that have nothing to do with the merits of the challenges. Faced with these odds, many potential challengers aren’t filing at all. Even After a Challenge Is Accepted, The USPTO Director Can Cancel It When the PTAB decides to hear an IPR case, that means the petition has been “instituted”—but that has never meant that the petitioner will definitely win. It means the PTAB has determined the challenge warrants a full merits review, and the parties could expect the proceeding to continue toward a final written decision. But under the current USPTO leadership, that expectation has disappeared. The PTAB’s institution decisions are being repeatedly vacated by the Director. USPTO Director John Squires has vacated at least 29 decisions granting institution of IPR proceedings, and subsequently denied the petitions, terminating those proceedings before a final written decision. These include cases that PTAB judges had already agreed to hear, as well as proceedings that Squires himself had previously allowed to proceed. This level of retroactive intervention is unprecedented. In some cases, the parties had already invested substantial time and money litigating before the PTAB, only to have the proceeding terminated based on new reasoning by the Director’s office that arose after institution. For example, in Revvo Technologies v. Cerebrum Sensor Technologies , the Director vacated an institution decision and remanded the case to the Board. The Board then instituted review again, but the Director reversed that decision. Using a new approach, the Director said that the petition had inconsistencies between claim construction positions taken before the PTAB and in district court. Since then, that decision has been cited as a basis for terminating several other instituted proceedings. The result is another layer of uncertainty for people who want to challenge bad patents. Getting through the front door of an institution decision is much harder than it used to be—and now, even getting through that door doesn’t mean the PTAB will decide your challenge. Predictability is one of the things that made IPRs work. Congress Created the PTAB To Avoid Costly Litigation Congress created IPRs in part because challenging a questionable patent in federal court is enormously expensive and risky. Patent examiners work under serious time constraints, and some patents that shouldn’t have been granted will inevitably issue. Not every patent dispute requires years of expensive district court litigation. Congress recognized that, and created an administrative process, staffed with experts more capable of correcting those mistakes. That system has benefited the public. Since 2012, it has helped invalidate thousands of patent claims that never should have been issued. The IPR process has protected startups, software developers, nonprofits, and small businesses that otherwise would have faced crushing litigation costs simply for building products or offering services that use everyday internet technology. EFF supports a balanced IPR system because it should be easier to fight against bogus patents that should never have been issued. The cost of fighting a patent can be a weapon in itself, and weak patents don't just burden large technology companies. Patent trolls routinely target small businesses and independent developers , and have gone after podcasters, retailers, and even coffee shops and nonprofits. These organizations have neither the resources nor the desire to spend years litigating over potentially invalid patents in federal court. IPR offers a chance to challenge those patents before litigation costs get out of control. If we weaken the IPR system, bad patents become much harder and more expensive to challenge. We Shouldn't Accept This as the New Normal Some defenders of the current approach argue that lower institution rates reflect more balance in the patent system. But institution rates at the PTAB have plummeted from 68% to 41% in just two years—a nearly 40% decline. IPR petition filings have reached historic lows. And even proceedings that have already been instituted can now be terminated months later, without a decision on the merits. These developments send a troubling message to members of the public who might want to use the PTAB: don't bother. The PTAB doesn’t need to institute every petition. But it does need to provide a process that is transparent, predictable, and fair. Right now, confidence in the system is disappearing. If companies, individuals, and nonprofits conclude that IPRs aren’t worth pursuing, the consequences won't stop at the PTAB. More weak patents that never should have been granted will survive, and patent trolls will use them. That means more defendants facing expensive district court litigation or paying settlements driven by the cost of litigation. That's not what Congress intended when it created IPRs . It should not become the PTAB's “new normal.”

In some cases, the parties had already invested substantial time and money litigating before the PTAB, only to have the proceeding terminated based on new reasoning by the Director’s office that arose after institution.

For example, in Revvo Technologies v. Cerebrum Sensor Technologies, the Director vacated an institution decision and remanded the case to the Board. The Board then instituted review again, but the Director reversed that decision. Using a new approach, the Director said that the petition had inconsistencies between claim construction positions taken before the PTAB and in district court. Since then, that decision has been cited as a basis for terminating several other instituted proceedings.

The result is another layer of uncertainty for people who want to challenge bad patents. Getting through the front door of an institution decision is much harder than it used to be—and now, even getting through that door doesn’t mean the PTAB will decide your challenge. Predictability is one of the things that made IPRs work.

Congress Created the PTAB To Avoid Costly Litigation

Congress created IPRs in part because challenging a questionable patent in federal court is enormously expensive and risky. Patent examiners work under serious time constraints, and some patents that shouldn’t have been granted will inevitably issue. Not every patent dispute requires years of expensive district court litigation. Congress recognized that, and created an administrative process, staffed with experts more capable of correcting those mistakes.

That system has benefited the public. Since 2012, it has helped invalidate thousands of patent claims that never should have been issued. The IPR process has protected startups, software developers, nonprofits, and small businesses that otherwise would have faced crushing litigation costs simply for building products or offering services that use everyday internet technology.

EFF supports a balanced IPR system because it should be easier to fight against bogus patents that should never have been issued. The cost of fighting a patent can be a weapon in itself, and weak patents don't just burden large technology companies. Patent trolls routinely target small businesses and independent developers, and have gone after podcasters, retailers, and even coffee shops and nonprofits. These organizations have neither the resources nor the desire to spend years litigating over potentially invalid patents in federal court. IPR offers a chance to challenge those patents before litigation costs get out of control.

If we weaken the IPR system, bad patents become much harder and more expensive to challenge.

We Shouldn't Accept This as the New Normal

Some defenders of the current approach argue that lower institution rates reflect more balance in the patent system. But institution rates at the PTAB have plummeted from 68% to 41% in just two years—a nearly 40% decline. IPR petition filings have reached historic lows. And even proceedings that have already been instituted can now be terminated months later, without a decision on the merits.

These developments send a troubling message to members of the public who might want to use the PTAB: don't bother. The PTAB doesn’t need to institute every petition. But it does need to provide a process that is transparent, predictable, and fair. Right now, confidence in the system is disappearing.

If companies, individuals, and nonprofits conclude that IPRs aren’t worth pursuing, the consequences won't stop at the PTAB. More weak patents that never should have been granted will survive, and patent trolls will use them. That means more defendants facing expensive district court litigation or paying settlements driven by the cost of litigation.

That's not what Congress intended when it created IPRs. It should not become the PTAB's “new normal.”

title: U.S. Supreme Court Deals Final Blow to Corporate Human Rights Accountability
text: For the past two decades, the U.S. Supreme Court has been slowly weakening the Alien Tort Statute (ATS) , a key human rights law that allows foreign nationals to sue persons or entities in civil court for harms resulting from violations of international law . The court’s recent ruling in Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe I dealt the law a final blow, foreclosing—absent new legislation by Congress—any future ability by plaintiffs to use the law to hold technology companies accountable for aiding and abetting human rights abuses. EFF filed multiple amicus briefs in the case , including most recently in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court Rejected New Causes of Action Under the ATS The ATS was passed by the very first Congress in 1789 and in just a few words gives U.S. federal courts jurisdiction to hear civil claims brought by foreign nationals against defendants who violated “the law of nations or a treaty of the United States." There has been a longstanding question about what counts as a valid civil claim under “the law of nations.” In Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain (2004), the Supreme Court had noted three historical international law claims that the First Congress likely had in mind: violation of safe conducts , infringement of the rights of ambassadors, and piracy, collectively known as the Blackstone Three . The Sosa court also held that federal courts may recognize other substantive causes of action under the ATS if they reflect international norms that are “specific, universal, and obligatory,” stating that this “door is still ajar subject to vigilant doorkeeping, and thus open to a narrow class of international norms today.” Thus, the Sosa court recognized that the ATS could be used to bring claims related to historical violations of international law as well as select newer claims reflecting modern concepts of human rights. In Cisco , the Supreme Court overruled the second Sosa holding. The majority held that the current case, a technology company aiding and abetting torture and other human rights abuses, was beyond the scope of the original three ATS claims and it was not for the court to create new ways of enforcing international law. The court said: [W]e close the door that Sosa cracked to judicially created ATS liability. We do not disturb Sosa ’s holding that the ATS is a jurisdictional statute; nor do we revisit its assumption that causes of action are available for torts corresponding to the Blackstone three. We conclude only that Sosa was overly optimistic in its prediction that there might be a narrow class of cases in which courts may create ATS actions without infringing on the prerogatives of the political branches. In truth, this class is a null set. What result for this case? Cisco argues that the Ninth Circuit erred in holding that aiding-and-abetting liability exists under the ATS for the torts alleged by the plaintiffs. Cisco is correct. Courts cannot create new rights of action to remedy violations of international law, so there is necessarily no liability for aiding and abetting such violations. Plaintiffs’ ATS claims against Cisco must be dismissed. Cisco is Off the Hook for Aiding and Abetting Horrific Human Rights Abuses The Supreme Court’s ending of the plaintiffs’ case against Cisco is hugely disappointing given that the case has been going on since 2011 and the Ninth Circuit in 2023 allowed the case to move forward in an excellent and well-reasoned opinion. The Ninth Circuit held, in part: We conclude that Plaintiffs’ allegations, accepted as true, are sufficient to state a plausible claim that Cisco provided essential technical assistance to the douzheng [ violent struggle ] of Falun Gong with awareness that the international law violations of torture, arbitrary detention, disappearance, and extrajudicial killing were substantially likely to take place . The plaintiffs sued Cisco for the company’s role in building and deploying the “Golden Shield,” also referred to as “The Great Firewall of China”—a vast surveillance system that Cisco began building in the late 1990s and that the company customized to enable the Chinese government to target disfavored minorities, including members of the Falun Gong religion. The thirteen plaintiffs —Falun Gong practitioners—alleged arrest, detention, and torture, including of themselves and family members, at least one of whom died by beating while being detained. The allegations were horrific: the plaintiffs were placed in forced labor camps, beaten with steel rods, shocked with electric batons, and endured sleep deprivation and violent force-feeding. Importantly, the plaintiffs also alleged that their private emails, text messages, and other information—intercepted by the Golden Shield—were shared with the torture sites, and shown to them and used as part of their torture and forced conversion sessions, which included threats to their family members and others who had communicated with them. And now, Cisco is off the hook for all of this. Congress Must Act to Hold American Tech Companies Accountable for Aiding and Abetting Human Rights Abuses As we argued in our amicus brief to the Supreme Court, a robust federal statute is necessary given that voluntary and informal mechanisms of corporate human rights accountability are inadequate. The plaintiffs filed their lawsuit in 2011. The following year, in 2012, Cisco first published its Global Human Rights Policy. Since then, the company has never provided redress to the plaintiffs, despite its currently operative human rights policy stating: Where we have identified that we have caused or contributed to an adverse human rights impact , we are committed to providing access to and cooperating in remediation for affected individuals, workers, and communities through legitimate processes. What’s more, the Associated Press conducted an extensive 2025 investigation , which recently won the Pulitzer Prize , further mapping Cisco’s and other American tech companies’ involvement in creating China’s surveillance state over the past three decades. When questioned by the AP reporters, the companies dismissed any notion of human rights obligations and simply “said they adhere to relevant export controls , laws and regulations where they operate.” In short, Cisco’s commitment to human rights is a fiction. Given that the U.S. Supreme Court has effectively read the ATS into non-existence, Congress must now step up. While there might be other avenues for redress including under state law, there must also be a comprehensive federal human rights law allowing any plaintiff to hold American companies—especially technology companies—accountable for aiding and abetting human rights abuses, with knowledge or intent that those abuses would occur, and whether the victims suffered those abuses in the U.S. or in foreign countries. The implications of this gap in U.S. human rights law are significant. As Prof. Harold Koh considered : [T]he Justices should ask whether affording such immunity in Cisco would implicitly signal to U.S. companies that they could not be held liable for assisting the U.S. government in committing gross violations. Such violations could include constructing a mass surveillance system that may be used to surveil, persecute, retaliate against, and punish real and perceived opponents and constructing systems that autonomously commit war crimes. American companies should not have a free pass to build out surveillance states (or other technologically sophisticated systems) that not only violate personal privacy or facilitate censorship, but that can also lead to real-world physical violence and even death. Related Cases: Doe I v. Cisco

title: Google Forcing AI on Students Is BS
text: Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school. Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini for 150 million K-12 students on Google Classroom, leaving educators scrambling to respond . A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators would also be turning off Google search . Google walked this back somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom. Tying AI to Search It’s no secret that the biggest companies in AI are operating at a huge loss , in the hope they can follow Uber’s enshittification playbook . Offer a cheap convenience at a major loss until old systems atrophy, then flip the script to reduce wages and raise consumer costs—whether that’s paying with cash or with data. This puts Google in the odd position of an incumbent, with around 90% of search traffic . It needs to not only make good on its own AI investment, but protect its dominance from new AI tools. It’s not just enough to offer its own AI mode, it needs to turn search into AI mode, while engaging in clumsy self-preferencing that is eating its own ad revenue . The problem with this approach is the public is split on AI, to put it mildly. Some users will welcome these changes, but the rest are stuck in an all-or-nothing bargain. Anyone concerned about the accuracy of AI overviews or their impact on click-through rates for online communities and small publishers can just deal with it . The bet is any inconvenience in switching to an alternative is enough to keep you trapped. Google can and should offer a way to disable AI overviews. Smaller services like DuckDuckGo* and Brave search have simple and persisting AI settings which don’t require login. These services also don't mince words and make a distinction between generated AI summaries, suspected AI results, and the backend use of AI to curate links. It’s not enough to point to opaque workarounds , either. Adding “-ai” to your Google search will usually remove AI Overview, but so will “-unicorn”. This trick isn’t meant to be an AI off-switch, it’s a quirk of how AI Overview was implemented and can change at any time. These tricks also don’t generalize well to settings for system administrators . Hacks might work for now, but everyone—including administrators—deserve clear set-and-forget controls for the tools they rely on. Pushing AI on Schools De-googling your life isn’t easy, and for schools it can be even more difficult. For decades Google has gone after schools to foster life-long Google users—resulting in many institutions being deeply entrenched in its ecosystem despite data privacy concerns . That’s because schools face major switching costs when moving to a competitor. It takes more than flipping a setting—it means a lengthy contract process, staff retraining, and a cumbersome migration of past work. The difficulty of switching makes granular controls even more essential, particularly for a hot-button issue like generative AI. Few parents would send their kids to AI-driven schools , but they may want their kids to learn tools like search as they exist outside of the classroom. However, many parents and teachers concerned with AI disrupting learning are pushing major school districts to implement temporary AI moratoriums for young students. These pauses are meant to make sure any introduction of AI fits the needs of students and is done in a way that actually makes sure educators are prepared. But in either camp, this is a choice that must be made by schools, not Google. Teachers know more about what their students need than a trillion-dollar tech company, and this expertise should be respected in their own classrooms. Google’s self-preferencing and desperate attempt to eventually recoup on an AI money pit must be tempered with more fine-tune controls over generative AI. It’s in Google’s own interest to stop abusing its dominance to piss off users, advertisers, and school communities. It’s also Google’s responsibility as an adjudicated monopolist. *DuckDuckGo is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

title: Presenting 'Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures'
text: What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real? Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. That's why earlier this year with the queer arts collective , we put out a call for submissions inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom. And we’re excited to share that the project is now live! Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution. These essays and stories remind us that digital rights aren't just about the existence of technology and its deployment as existing in a vacuum, but instead about how tech tools are a way for people to express themselves freely, find communities, explore identities, and build spaces to exist and seek joy without fear. Too often, conversations about technology focus on innovation, efficiency, and the next big thing while overlooking the people and communities most affected by the systems being built. This project was an effort to break containment and make space for something different: a chance to imagine digital futures rooted in queer creativity, resistance, and possibility. Together with the queer arts collective, we were excited to launch the magazine and celebrate the artists and ideas that brought it to life through our session at Mozilla Festival last week, ‘ Privacy x Queer Desire ,’ where we started out by co-curating a community privacy plan grounded in digital fairness before launching the magazine. If the stories in Encoding Queer Digital Futures teach us one thing, it’s that we don't have to accept the digital future handed to us by oppressive governments and tech companies. We already have pre-Big Tech internet experiences encoded in our fondest memories that can inform our dreams for something better, and together we can build a new reality. Read Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures here .

title: EFF Submission to OHCHR Consultation on Child Rights and Safety in the Digital Environment
text: “ The safety of young people in the digital environment cannot be assessed without also considering the safety of young people in offline environments. For millions of young people around the world, the digital environment is their safe place, their haven from an unsafe physical environment, community, or family situation. The digital environment may be the best, perhaps only, place for them to find critical safety information and community, to explore ideas that are controversial in their families and larger physical environments, and to otherwise nourish their personal autonomy. “For these young people, regulatory efforts that limit their access to online services or to certain features they find valuable, make their lives, in total, less safe, even if there has been some marginal safety benefit to their digital environment. “The OHCHR must thus consider the whole of young persons' lives in any recommendations that come out of this process and not treat ‘safety, physical or mental health, and rights in the digital environment’ as disconnected from safety, physical or mental health, and rights elsewhere.” So begins EFF’s submission to the global Call for Inputs on Child Rights and Safety in the Digital Environment conducted by the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner on Human Rights. The OHCHR is preparing a report on the issue to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council at its 64th session in the first quarter of 2027. The Human Rights Council requested the OHCHR to solicit input from a wide range of stakeholders, including child and youth perspectives, and convene five regional consultations to assess the risks to the safety of the child in the digital environment and best practices to address these risks in different geographical areas, bearing in mind current and emerging business models. The OHCHR acknowledges that young people today navigate a digital environment with both “unprecedented opportunities” and “serious and evolving risks,” and sets out a rights-based framing whereby “Children's 'safety' is therefore addressed through the full framework of their rights — with freedom from violence (Art. 19) and protection from exploitation and abuse (Arts. 34–36) as clearly defined obligations, situated alongside privacy (Art. 16), access to information (Arts. 13 and 17), expression (Art. 13), participation (Art. 12), and development (Art. 6). Protection and the full range of children's rights are understood as reinforcing rather than competing imperatives, and measures taken in the name of safety must not be used to restrict the enjoyment of other rights, such as the right to privacy and the right to participate.” In light of this, EFF’s submission focused on the current general disregard for young people's speech and privacy rights by regulators around the world, all of whom seem far more interested in empowering parents rather than young people themselves, or meaningfully involving young people in the regulatory process. We emphasized the human rights-centered uses young people make of social media that were not specifically set out in the concept note. We also explained that too often, policy proposals aiming to remedy the issues of online safety for young people introduce limitations on access to online services and content rather than tackling the specific problems that people experience. More specifically, our submission looks at: the most significant risks to young people’s safety in the digital environment how digital product design and business models drive risks to children's rights online, including in AI-mediated services the inclusion of young people’s views in the design, governance, and regulation of digital environments how equality and non-discrimination in access and protection can be ensured the promotion of digital literacy, skills, and empowerment for young people the impact of legislative and regulatory measures from the United States to Indonesia and Australia importance of broader, more systemic interventions that can address address online harms how global instruments and processes can protect young people online. The internet is where young people learn, find community, explore their identities, access important information, and express themselves. Curtailing these opportunities doesn't make them safer. And requiring everyone to hand over sensitive personal information just to access online spaces creates privacy risks for all users. For millions of young people around the world, the digital environment is their safe place, their haven from an unsafe physical environment, community, or family situation. The digital environment may be the best, perhaps only, place for them to find critical safety information and community, to explore ideas that are controversial in their families and larger physical environments, and to otherwise nourish their personal autonomy.

“For these young people, regulatory efforts that limit their access to online services or to certain features they find valuable, make their lives, in total, less safe, even if there has been some marginal safety benefit to their digital environment.

“The OHCHR must thus consider the whole of young persons' lives in any recommendations that come out of this process and not treat ‘safety, physical or mental health, and rights in the digital environment’ as disconnected from safety, physical or mental health, and rights elsewhere.”

The OHCHR is preparing a report on the issue to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council at its 64th session in the first quarter of 2027. The Human Rights Council requested the OHCHR to solicit input from a wide range of stakeholders, including child and youth perspectives, and convene five regional consultations to assess the risks to the safety of the child in the digital environment and best practices to address these risks in different geographical areas, bearing in mind current and emerging business models.

title: When the Watchdogs Are Silenced: India's Crackdown on Those Documenting Online Censorship
text: On November 3, our colleagues at the Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in) received notifications from X that the Delhi Police had issued takedown requests targeting 42 URLs. Among the accounts and posts targeted were those belonging to SFLC.in , the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), and X account @geoblockedindia, as well as posts documenting legal notices and instances of online censorship. Takedown requests targeting SFLC.in and other digital rights groups threaten not only their work, but the public’s ability to know when and how online speech is being restricted. The requests cite grounds including hate speech, alleged defamation of the Hindu nationalist organization Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), and concerns relating to safety and security. But the context in which these requests have emerged is particularly troubling: they target organizations and individuals whose work involves documenting restrictions on online expression and making those restrictions visible to the public. In other words, the organizations being targeted are among those trying to tell the public when and how its speech is being censored. SFLC.in is one of India's most important digital rights organizations and promotes innovation and open access to knowledge by helping developers make great free and open-source software, protects privacy and civil liberties for Indians by educating and providing free legal advice, and helps policymakers make informed and just decisions about use of technology. In 2025, we recognized their work with an EFF Award for Defending Digital Freedoms. IFF (the Internet Freedom Foundation) is another of EFF's close allies in India. Like EFF, IFF combines advocacy campaigns and strategic litigation to advance digital rights. They write frequently about internet shutdowns and have filed several lawsuits contesting them. Among SFLC.in's initiatives is its Free Speech Tracker , which documents instances of online censorship, content restrictions, and account takedowns in India. In a country where government orders to restrict online content are often opaque, this work is absolutely essential. Recent legal notices object to the tracker itself, as well as the organization’s documentation of restricted content and geo-blocked material. The allegations against SFLC.in include claims that it is "continuously opposing government directions" and publicly circulating information about restricted content, thereby undermining measures taken in the name of national security and public order. But documenting government censorship is not the same as undermining public safety. Reporting that content has been restricted is not an endorsement of that content, nor does it constitute an attempt to circumvent the law. It is an exercise in transparency and accountability, and one that allows journalists, researchers, civil society organizations, and the public to understand how governments exercise their power over the information landscape. Censorship thrives in the absence of transparency The use of legal complaints and platform takedown mechanisms against organizations documenting censorship creates a particularly troubling dynamic. When those who monitor restrictions on expression are threatened with having their accounts or reporting removed, the result is a chilling effect that extends far beyond the immediate targets. Other organizations or journalists may think twice before documenting controversial takedowns or challenging government orders, and the public loses access to an independent record of decisions that affect its ability to speak and access information online. There is also an important role here for platforms like X. Platforms must be transparent about the requests they receive, provide meaningful notice to affected users, and ensure that any restrictions are subject to appropriate scrutiny and avenues for appeal. When governments seek to restrict speech, platforms have a responsibility to avoid becoming opaque intermediaries through which censorship is quietly carried out. These developments are part of a broader pattern of pressure on independent civil society organizations working to defend freedom of expression and access to information in India. Digital rights groups play an indispensable role in documenting the effects of government policies, identifying patterns of censorship, and challenging restrictions that undermine fundamental rights. Their ability to do so independently is not a peripheral concern; it is a cornerstone of a healthy democratic society. The right to freedom of expression includes the right to scrutinize the exercise of government power. That includes the right to document censorship, question the reasons given for it, and make that information available to the public. EFF stands in solidarity with SFLC.in, the Internet Freedom Foundation, @geoblockedindia, and all those working to document and challenge restrictions on online expression in India. We urge the authorities in India to respect the rights of digital rights organizations to conduct their work without intimidation or retaliation, and to ensure that any restrictions on online expression comply with international human rights standards.

title: Reflecting on Digital Rights Wins and Losses in Sacramento
text: California’s 2026 legislative session has officially adjourned and it’s time to reflect on the wins and losses that have shaped Californians’ digital rights landscape this year. This was the second year of a two-year legislative session, which meant several bills resumed their legislative paths from 2025 . EFF monitored nearly 100 bills in the state over the two-year session. These included proposed regulations on 3D printers, access to social media platforms, police, commercial, and workplace surveillance practices, AI, and other privacy concerns. While we saw some victories, alarming developments also raised serious concerns about the future of privacy protection in the state. Celebrating Wins Use of automated decision-making and surveillance in the workplace Governor Newsom signed vital protections on the use of automated decision-making in the workplace and workplace surveillance tools, specifically No Robo Bosses ( SB 947 ) and AB 1883 . Championed by our labor partners , SB 947 limits how employers can use automated decision-making to fire or discipline workers, including provisions that ensure workers get vital information about automated decisions that affect them, and that an algorithm is not the only authority for these consequential decisions. Alongside it, AB 1883 prohibits the use of workplace surveillance to predict emotions or collect neural data. This stops employers from using potentially biased, invasive, and exploitative forms of AI surveillance at the workplace, marking an important step toward creating workplaces that respect the privacy and autonomy of workers. We look forward to continuing to ensure that technology in California’s workplaces is deployed fairly, thoughtfully, and with respect for all workers. Protecting against federal overreach EFF was also grateful to see Governor Newsom sign SB 747 , which allows damages lawsuits against federal officials who violate the U.S. Constitution . Victims of constitutional violations deserve a complete remedy and this law also helps deter constitutional violations in the first place. Gaps in current law often make it difficult to seek a damages remedy against federal officials who violate the U.S. Constitution. This bill makes it easier to bring such litigation. Federal law enforcement officials have violated our First Amendment right to record on-duty police and other newsworthy subjects, and also sometimes violate our Fourth Amendment right to be free from unreasonable searches of our phones and laptops . When this happens, the people who suffer these violations should be able to sue these officials for damages . Additionally, EFF supported two bills (which are now state law) that clarify and extend California’s shield laws to protect patients, healthcare providers, and others involved in reproductive healthcare and gender-affirming care that is legal in California. After the overturn of Roe v. Wade , California enacted numerous shield laws to protect people who provide, receive, or help others obtain healthcare that is legal in California. These laws prohibit California agencies and certain companies from helping other states enforce laws that punish this care. Yet the federal government and coordinated efforts in other states still threaten access to these legally protected healthcare services. AB 1854 addresses these threats by expanding coverage to more California businesses and individuals who receive legal demands, creating a notification process so the Attorney General can intervene to stop improper disclosures, and clarifying that law enforcement cannot arrest someone if the Governor refuses an extradition request. These protections serve as a necessary response to real and escalating tactics outside the state targeting lawful reproductive healthcare. EFF also supported AB 1930 to protect confidential medical records from politically motivated investigations into lawful healthcare, empowering the California Attorney General’s office to meaningfully intervene and respond to out-of-state subpoenas or requests for data regarding protected care. Young people online EFF is dedicated to protecting the rights of young people online. We supported a handful of bills on digital literacy and cybersecurity education that were signed into law, such as AB 2071 on digital wellness instruction and AB 2298 on cybersecurity in educational standards. Unlike blanket bans , these bills address online safety through education rather than prohibition. Young people rely on the internet not just for entertainment, but for civic engagement , education , self-expression , and community —especially vulnerable youth who may lack support in their physical surroundings. Real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation. Research consistently shows that open, honest conversations about digital literacy and privacy with trusted adults are far more effective at protecting youth than restrictive censorship laws. Young people themselves recognize this need; in fact, AB 2071 was co-authored by a group of students actively seeking better resources to navigate their digital lives safely. EFF and our allies were also able to stop the expansion of California’s dangerous age gating law from operating systems to browsers. The California legislature stepped back from their plan to expand the 2025 age-gating law and ultimately removed language from AB 1856 that could have compounded serious threats to users’ speech, privacy, and security just to browse the internet, and positively, removed the burdens on open-source operating systems. Real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation While EFF still believes the underlying law that AB 1856 amends, AB 1043, is unconstitutional , we appreciate that the legislature did not expand this problematic age-gating framework to browsers. We were also pleased that an earlier amendment to AB 1856 reduced the threat to the open-source community by exempting open-source operating systems. Given these changes, EFF removed its opposition to AB 1856, and thanks the author for listening to concerns from advocates and developers. Mourning Losses Updating California’s Information Practices Act (IPA) EFF was proud to co-sponsor AB 1337 this session alongside our friends at Oakland Privacy and Assemblymember Chris Ward, who is also the chair of the legislative LGBTQ Caucus. The bill unfortunately failed to cross the finish line after stalling in the Senate. AB 1337 would have updated California's foundational Information Practices Act of 1977 and extended its vital privacy safeguards present at the state agency level to counties and cities. Today, city and county governments collect vast amounts of sensitive personal data (from public health records such as vaccinations, to welfare assistance details, to license plate reader data) and administer programs that were likely not contemplated back in 1977. Yet the law has simply not kept up with modern data practices, and California still has no state law governing how local governments handle this information. While we could not build enough political progress to pass the bill this session, closing this local privacy gap remains an urgent need for California. Social media ban Another major setback was the passage (and subsequent signing ) of a social media ban for youth under the age of 16 ( AB 1709 ). Technology and the laws that regulate it should support and empower young people, but AB 1709 falls far short of this goal. Using technology is how we learn and build community in today’s world, but laws such as AB 1709 cut young people off from essential information and experiences . They also particularly harm those already facing increased challenges who find safety in supportive online communities that they cannot always access in the physical world. Technology and the laws that regulate it should support and empower young people Denying minors access to digital forums or stripping out basic tools needed to navigate them will not make young people safer or healthier in the AI age. Research shows social media bans are ineffectual while denying young people opportunities to develop their own voices, share their art, practice religion, or engage in politics. These laws also hurt all of us. Age-gating requirements force everyone to give up more personal information . To verify who can pass through online gates, companies will collect even more data, concentrating power in corporate hands rather than protecting people. AB 1709 is also inconsistent with rights to free expression , meaning California will spend resources defending a law that will likely get tied up in court . Gutting California’s Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA) CIPA was originally intended to protect personal privacy against surveillance and included a private right of action so consumers could hold corporations accountable in court. This is why EFF and allied organizations spent the two-year session strongly opposing SB 690 —a bill we dubbed the " Corporate Cover-Up Act " for its attempt to weaken consumer protections in CIPA. Although SB 690 was narrowed from its original draft , we asked Governor Newsom to veto it because it strips away the law's private right of action—a vital tool for individuals fighting back against unlawful metadata surveillance. People deserve the right to decide whether to bring a lawsuit , which remains one of the most effective ways to deter corporate abuse. Unfortunately, the Governor signed the bill and even urged the legislature to go further next year. It's especially alarming to see this disregard for accountability as the federal government and law enforcement agencies seek data from businesses or data brokers to target people based on political beliefs, religious affiliations, or health decisions. We expect to see further attacks on CIPA next legislative session, as Governor Newsom’s signing statement called for “additional work in this area” and urged the legislature to “take this on next year to ensure a fair balance between protecting private information and preventing rapacious litigation." Banning the sale of sensitive personal information California also missed the opportunity to join other states in restricting the sale of sensitive data. We are deeply disappointed that Governor Newsom vetoed AB 1542 , which would have ensured sensitive personal information stays private by banning its sale outright. There's a nationwide movement to protect consumers by making intimate details off-limits for businesses to sell or share. From precise geolocation and genetic data to private messages, health records, sexual orientation, and immigration status, sensitive data reveals the most private aspects of our lives. Monetizing this information fuels financial scams, predatory pricing, and warrant-free government surveillance. By vetoing this bill , California not only fails to lead but falls behind other states, by missing a critical opportunity to protect our most vulnerable communities. 3D printing The California legislature unfortunately also passed AB 2047 , which aimed to make every 3D printer come pre-loaded with censorship software . It's a law that is trying to prevent an act that is already illegal in the state , and just won't work . It was part of a recent sweep of misguided state bills which purport to go after "ghost guns," but actually “enshittify” 3D printers by introducing privacy risks and a new way to restrict or upcharge users. Lawmakers even considered including misdemeanor charges that would have impacted people using alternative open-source programs. Fortunately an outpouring of opposition from makers and civil liberties advocates resulted in a bill so limited that, despite having passed and been signed into law, will not affect makers until ASTM International publishes a standard — something the organization had not been considering doing . Where California Missed the Mark Consumer privacy California lawmakers also missed key opportunities to curb commercial surveillance. EFF supported AB 2564 , which prohibits retailers from engaging in surveillance pricing , the invasive practice that allows corporations to offer the same product to two different people at two different prices based on scrutiny of their personal data. Unfortunately, the bill stalled on the last day of session. The legislature also failed to move AB 322 , which would have safeguarded the privacy of Californians by placing restrictions on the collection, use, and sale of location data. Last year, EFF published a rubric for comprehensive location privacy laws , outlining baseline standards states should meet to shield individuals from pervasive location surveillance. Since then, states like Connecticut, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, and Virginia have enacted new consumer privacy restraints on geolocation data . Yet, even as these states move the ball forward, most of their laws leave significant gaps that still must be filled. California failed to make that change and protect residents from location surveillance. Automatic license plate readers California lawmakers have lagged in enacting meaningful limits on automated license plate readers with all proposed ALPR regulation bills failing to pass since 2022. SB 1013 initially appeared on track to pass with broad support, but ultimately stalled in the final days of the session. EFF maintains high standards for ALPR legislation , favoring full bans or, at minimum , strict warrant requirements and brief data retention limits. While we remained neutral on earlier versions of SB 1013, EFF and our partners ultimately opposed the bill after late amendments compromised key privacy protections. The final draft would have doubled the current data retention period and allowed agencies to archive rather than delete data unrelated to active investigations—effectively shifting away from data minimization toward indefinite retention. (We saw San Francisco adopt a similar proposal this year ). We encourage California lawmakers to draw from our ALPR legislative agenda to enact robust safeguards or ban ALPR mass surveillance altogether. Looking Ahead Next session, we expect ALPR legislation to be top of mind as states across the country reckon with the harms the technology has caused. We will also be monitoring the results and action following the state’s audit into California’s fusion centers . Following calls from advocates to address privacy abuses and a lack of transparency, the Joint Legislative Audit Committee approved Senator Sabrina Cervantes’ audit request in March 2026. This builds on our past experiences working with JLAC audits to expose law enforcement overreach—such as the state auditor's damning 2020 report on law enforcement’s use of automated license plate readers and our 2016 push to fix the deeply flawed CalGang database . The audit will examine the legal authority, governance, and funding of the centers, map out state and private data systems accessed by personnel, and review protocols for handling data breaches and unauthorized surveillance. This audit will mark the first comprehensive review of these facilities in 13 years and should be released by Summer 2027. We hope lawmakers use the findings to rein in these centers and their unauthorized surveillance. Other “zombie bills” are also expected to return next year, including legislation regarding the use of copyrighted material to train AI systems. Throughout the two-year session, EFF raised serious concerns about AB 412 , a bill that would require AI developers to identify and disclose copyrighted works used in generative AI training. We argued that complying with such a mandate is practically impossible , as it demands information that often does not exist and cannot realistically be obtained. While we are glad the legislature paused to consider the best approach rather than rushing this policy forward, we expect legislation targeting fair use and AI training to return next session. More broadly on AI, vulnerabilities and security issues have dominated recent news cycles, and everyday Californians feel real anxiety about the risks of AI. We expect to see numerous bills addressing issues like existential risk and kill switches , as Assembly and Senate privacy committees in California have held informational hearings on these topics over the last month. We hope to work with legislators to address the threats of AI and ensure that technology supports rights, justice, freedom, and innovation for all people. Laws should always ensure that technology empowers rather than oppresses.
