title: Anti-Circumvention Laws Raise the Cost of Knowledge
text: The vast amount of information on the open web requires researchers and journalists to adapt with new tools to make sense of it all. Checking facts, gauging public opinion, and other lines of inquiry depend on being able to analyze the overwhelming amount of material posted online every day. Unfortunately, responding to the AI industry’s voracious appetite for data, companies stewarding this public data are looking to cash in and block access to the open web. This makes the web harder to navigate, and threatens all kinds of important research. Reddit’s lawsuit against SerpAPI[1] and Perplexity threatens to do exactly that. Reddit was once a very open platform, fostering a community of alternative apps and extensions putting users in control of their experience. Since the rise of AI however, it changed tack. Over the last three years Reddit has closed APIs to users , limited UI features , and otherwise restrained access without login . By making the voices on the platform harder to access, the company has positioned itself as a gatekeeper, and has since struck a lucrative data-sharing arrangement with Google. SerpAPI, in contrast, is a tool which offers automated access to Google’s search engine results pages. It’s used by Perplexity, an AI-based search tool. Reddit sued to stop SerpAPI and Perplexity from bypassing Reddit’s own arrangement with Google. (Google brought a similar suit, which was dismissed by another court.) It comes as little surprise that the legal weapon Reddit employed in this case is Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act, the same “anti-circumvention” law that has caused so much trouble for artists, innovators, and researchers over the years—and that EFF has fought against from the beginning. Reddit’s suit claimed that SerpAPI’s use of widely used techniques to access Google search results amounted to “circumventing” access controls on copyrighted works. There are major problems with this argument. First, Reddit doesn’t own the copyright in its users’ posts—the users do, and they grant Reddit the right to distribute the posted content freely. Second, there’s no meaningful copyright infringement going on here. Perplexity functions like a search engine, responding to users’ queries with relevant links and optionally an AI-generated summary. Crawling and indexing the web to create a search engine was long ago ruled a fair use under copyright law. And third, Google’s efforts to put rate limits on search queries and block some kinds of automated querying aren’t the sort of “access controls” that Section 1201 was written for. The law was passed in 1998 and targeted things like breaking the encryption on DVDs and other digital media. In contrast to physical or paywalled media, Reddit posts are visible to everyone, without a paywall and generally without a login. Unfortunately, a federal district judge ruled in July that the suit could proceed, concluding that Section 1201 applied. That’s a dangerous ruling, because it casts a cloud of legal uncertainty over lots of important research, including efforts to study public sentiment through social media and to preserve records of historical events. Without tools that can look at the web at scale, many kinds of research are simply impossible today. But if employing those tools risks Section 1201 liability, only the wealthiest institutions will be able to use them. We cannot let the internet be rebuilt such that information is divided up among a handful of gatekeepers and sold back to us like cable subscription packages. If our knowledge of the online world comes only through wealthy institutions, the cost of knowledge will only increase and access to unbiased answers diminishes. [1] SerpAPI is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

title: The Vulnerability Apocalypse and Why We Should Fund Open Source
text: If you use the internet at all, you may have noticed that a large percentage of sites suddenly went down earlier this week — and all your nerdiest friends were talking about "The Vulnerability Apocalypse” and this thing called PHP that powers nearly 70% of the websites on the internet . You may find yourself wondering: what is PHP, what just happened, what is the vulnerability apocalypse, and what do I need to do? To find out what you can personally do read the first blog post in this series! What Is PHP? PHP is a programming language used mainly to create interactive websites. Facebook, Wordpress, Wikipedia, Etsy, and other major sites all use or were originally built on PHP. It is a long-established mainstay of web development. But because it is open-source, maintenance of these critical systems depends on a small number of volunteers working on this in their free time. The disaster scenario that happened this past week is the perfect example of why we need more money and people supporting open-source projects. Corporations should be contributing both. What Is the Vulnerability Apocalypse? Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) are the way that security professionals file reports about vulnerabilities in software. The National Vulnerability Database (NVD), run by NIST, is the official national database of CVEs. In other words, CVE reports managed by NIST are the closest thing we have to a canonical database of security vulnerabilities in software. The NVD currently has around 400,000 CVEs that have been filed and accepted since 1988. In just the month of October, 13,000 new CVEs have been submitted. This means that 3% of critical software security bugs that have ever been officially logged were found in the last month alone. And it's likely that by the end of the year over a quarter of the software vulnerabilities that have ever been found will be from 2026. Computer vulnerabilities reported are rising exponentially. Source: CVE Tracker This research is being driven almost entirely by the cybersecurity capabilities of major AI models from companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Historically it has been popularly assumed by cybersecurity experts that finding unknown (zero-day) exploits in any specific project and turning them into exploits was expensive. The knowledge to discover them was not widespread, and it was a hard task even for those initiated into the arcane ways of vulnerability hunting. Google even dedicated an entire team to it . But now thanks to major AI models, vulnerabilities are cheap, and anyone of moderate technical skill with a few dollars and access to a frontier AI model can find vulnerabilities in a few minutes. For example, recent vulnerabilities in PHP were found with a prompt to an AI model that literally said " find bad vulnerabilities in PHP ." What Happened This Week? In 2024, a potentially severe vulnerability in PHP was discovered during an external security audit . PHP’s maintainers couldn’t agree on a solution, but more importantly, they couldn’t find a way to exploit the vulnerability. Because it didn’t seem like an active threat, they ended up deprioritizing a fix in favor of working on more urgent security issues. Then, in August 2026, security researchers working with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic independently discovered the vulnerability again, and another one — and now, with a way to exploit them. We now know that the vulnerabilities were so severe that they would have allowed even moderately inventive hackers to take over any website that uses PHP and then steal customer data, launch further malware attacks, spy on users, take websites offline, or launch a massive denial of service attack. [ 1 ] Because of the severity of these vulnerabilities, several of the involved researchers got together with the makers of PHP to patch the vulnerabilities and disclose them in a coordinated manner. The idea was that hopefully everyone would get a chance to quietly release and then apply fixes for the vulnerabilities before the whole world found out about it. But news already started to leak on October 20th. There was a post on a widely read forum “Hacker News” and other posts elsewhere. One of the researchers accidentally published a video early. Companies reported seeing active exploitation of the vulnerabilities going back as far as October 17th. On October 21st, six hours before the planned press embargo, one company, Chainguard, jumped the gun and released a patch early, essentially giving anyone instructions about exactly where to find the vulnerabilities and how to weaponize them. This sent system administrators everywhere scrambling to patch their systems before they were taken over by hackers. And it’s going to take a long time to patch all these systems. At the time of this writing over 33 million websites are still running on vulnerable versions of PHP . The internet is run largely on open-source software, mostly maintained by a small handful of skilled volunteers occasionally getting a small stipend, not by major corporations and highly paid engineers. These are projects you have perhaps never heard of, like PHP, OpenSSL, and SQLite, but these programs run on nearly every computer in the world and are maintained by teams as small as one person. When a vulnerability is found in these projects, it can be devastating. PHP isn’t the only critical open-source software with a high severity vulnerability this week either. Other widespread open-source projects like Node.js and GitLab also had severe security bugs reported. The small number of already overworked open-source maintainers are now facing a deluge of vulnerability reports, some of which are false, but many of which are very real. Burnout in open source has never been higher . We Need Stronger Support for Open Source Projects Much of the foundation for the modern multibillion-dollar internet industry is built on open-source products that were created and still maintained — for free — by dedicated volunteers in their spare time. It’s an imperfect system, and it can lead to errors. One of those critical, under resourced open-source products is PHP. And while vulnerabilities in PHP were privately found years ago, they were left unfixed because they didn’t seem as impactful as other bugs at the time. These same vulnerabilities were recently rediscovered and proved to be trivially exploitable by security researchers using advanced AI models. While in the middle of the widespread, global effort to correct this mistake and deploy fixes, the problem was leaked by some of the security researchers who had gotten early access to the fixes. Unfortunately, this left millions of websites, ranging from personal blogs to government sites, vulnerable to hacking that could result in data theft, malware distribution, and worse. Open-source projects like PHP and others are the backbone of the entire internet. If they don’t get the resources they need, they and the internet they power, are at risk of falling apart. Corporations (whose products would not exist without these products) should be actively contributing to their maintenance. 1. A technical analysis of the vulnerabilities is out of scope for this post and has already been written by the original researchers .

These are projects you have perhaps never heard of, like PHP, OpenSSL, and SQLite, but these programs run on nearly every computer in the world and are maintained by teams as small as one person. When a vulnerability is found in these projects, it can be devastating.  

PHP isn’t the only critical open-source software with a high severity vulnerability this week either. Other widespread open-source projects like Node.js and GitLab also had severe security bugs reported.  

The small number of already overworked open-source maintainers are now facing a deluge of vulnerability reports, some of which are false, but many of which are very real. Burnout in open source has never been higher.  

We Need Stronger Support for Open Source Projects

Much of the foundation for the modern multibillion-dollar internet industry is built on open-source products that were created and still maintained—for free—by dedicated volunteers in their spare time. It’s an imperfect system, and it can lead to errors.  

One of those critical, under resourced open-source products is PHP. And while vulnerabilities in PHP were privately found years ago, they were left unfixed because they didn’t seem as impactful as other bugs at the time. These same vulnerabilities were recently rediscovered and proved to be trivially exploitable by security researchers using advanced AI models. While in the middle of the widespread, global effort to correct this mistake and deploy fixes, the problem was leaked by some of the security researchers who had gotten early access to the fixes. Unfortunately, this left millions of websites, ranging from personal blogs to government sites, vulnerable to hacking that could result in data theft, malware distribution, and worse.  

Open-source projects like PHP and others are the backbone of the entire internet. If they don’t get the resources they need, they and the internet they power, are at risk of falling apart. Corporations (whose products would not exist without these products) should be actively contributing to their maintenance.

title: Computer Security Is About to Get a Lot Worse, Here’s What You Can Do
text: It is a commonly held truth among computer geeks that there is no such thing as bug-free software, or a secure computer. Any piece of software that anyone actually uses will have a security vulnerability somewhere in the code . The more complex that software is, the more likely there will be a vulnerability. Fortunately for everyone, finding severe vulnerabilities was generally considered an expensive and difficult task requiring years of training and deep knowledge of how computers and software worked. Until recently there was a steady background hum of vulnerabilities being found and patched, with major vulnerabilities that could cripple the entire internet only happening every few years. Now that is no longer the case. You may have noticed your nerdiest friends freaking out about the “Vulnerability Apocalypse” this week and waving their arms in panic about something called PHP. You may have also noticed that some of your favorite websites were down for a bit. In the last two weeks of October alone, there have been multiple, potentially internet-breaking vulnerabilities reported and patched. Many of those vulnerabilities were in the open-source software that is the foundation of the vast majority of the internet. For more detailed information on what happened, and why supporting open-source projects matters, check out our other blog . This is all because frontier AI models, such as those created by OpenAI, Anthropic, and others, have made it incredibly cheap and easy to find previously unknown vulnerabilities (zero-days) in open- and closed-source code. Three percent of all software vulnerabilities ever found in history were found just in the month of October. This year alone researchers have found nearly a quarter of all software security issues which have ever been discovered. If exploiting critical software is now cheaper and easier than ever, what does that mean for us as individuals and what does that mean for society as a whole? TL; DR : It’s going to get worse before it gets better. But you can protect yourself with basic digital security hygiene that is now more important than ever. What Do I Need to Do? There absolutely needs to be a bigger conversation about how we got here and how to fix the systemic issues involved, including how corporations that depend on open-source code should contribute to their upkeep, and how big tech should be regulated. But for now, this news is a compelling reason to tighten up your digital hygiene. A lot of computers are going to get hacked a lot more often, and unfortunately, it isn’t going to get better any time soon. Thankfully, EFF has compiled a comprehensive set of security advice in our Surveillance Self-Defense guides . To start , we recommend making sure your browser and all applications are always up to date with the latest patches. You should also consider installing a tracker blocking tool, like EFF’s Privacy Badger ( now on Safari ), and remain vigilant for phishing attempts . Additionally, install a password manager and use unique passwords for each website, so that if one site is compromised, the rest of your passwords are safe. You should also be aware that data breaches may now be more likely, and the websites you visit may experience more attacks than usual, which means that some services may be disrupted. If you host a blog or other website, make sure that either you or your hosting provider has patched this particular issue. For additional tips on protecting yourself and others, head over to our Surveillance Self-Defense site . Additionally, if you’d like to support any of EFF’s open-source projects like Privacy Badger , Rayhunter , and Certbot , visit our donate page .

title: Two States Can Now Restrict Social Media Access—Here’s What To Do Next
text: Last week, two federal appeals courts issued opinions that will allow Florida and Georgia to start enforcing laws that will age-gate and block young people from accessing social media. The laws do not adequately respect minors’ rights to play, speak, and learn online. More fundamentally, these laws don’t help young people stay safe online—a goal that lawmakers should pursue. Age-Gated? Email EFF at agegates@eff.org . Because of the new laws, some young people will lose their ability to access lawful information, find their online communities, and even engage with school board members. Others will need parental permission to stay online. And adults will face increased demands to prove their age, which will put their privacy at increased risk simply to continue to use the services they already use. We opposed these laws because they threaten the free expression and privacy of both minors and adults. Even though these lawsuits are not over, the injunctions that paused enforcement have been lifted, and the states of Florida and Georgia will now be able to enforce broad restrictions on social media use. The restrictions that these states will start enforcing are a setback for the rights of all internet users, but they are not written in stone. That’s why EFF is encouraging internet users - and particularly young people – to start keeping a record of how they are affected. If you are a teenager who loses access to an online discussion, can’t participate in a political campaign, or stop seeking information because you don’t want to upload personal information, document what happened. The same is true for adults who may be mistakenly blocked by age checks, and parents who may encounter obstacles to authorizing their children's use of online services. These experiences matter. They can help us show courts, policymakers, and the public what government restrictions on online expression actually cost the people who live under them. Hopefully, with enough proof of the expressive harms these laws cause, we can push lawmakers to rescind them. That’s why we’re encouraging folks to reach out to EFF once they’ve documented these harms. You can write to us about this issue at the email address agegates@eff.org . The Decisions These two opinions, issued by the same panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit, allow Florida and Georgia to enforce restrictions on social media accounts for people under 16 years old. The requirements differ by state. In Florida , the judges allowed that state’s H.B. 3 to move forward, which requires covered platforms to ban anyone under 14 from opening or keeping accounts—even with parental permission. Teenagers who are 14 or 15 can have accounts only with parental consent. To be covered, a platform has to use algorithms, allow content uploads or the viewing of other peoples’ content, and have at least one feature on a list of features the state considers bad, including livestreaming, engagement metrics, autoplay, infinite scrolling, or push notifications. These requirements effectively apply to every major social media service that young people use. To the extent there is a silver lining in the ruling on Florida’s law, it’s that the panel recognized that H.B. 3 targets expression protected by the First Amendment. The problem is that the ruling uncritically accepts the idea that a social media service is addictive in a clinical sense, even if just 10% of users under 16 are using the platform for two or more hours per day (the standard set in H.B. 3). The court simply accepts that time spent online is a proxy for harm. The bill doesn’t distinguish doomscrolling or compulsive use from organizing a campaign, making art, or talking with friends. In Georgia , S.B. 351 can now be enforced. That law requires parental consent for anyone under 16 to hold an account on social media platforms. It also requires platforms to make “commercially reasonable efforts” to check users’ ages, which creates a hurdle for adults as well as under-16s. The ruling acknowledges that S.B. 351 “overwhelmingly applies to platforms that overwhelmingly host protected speech.” But the ruling faults the plaintiffs for not being able to show that “invalid applications substantially outweigh the valid ones.” That asks the groups challenging the law to meet a virtually impossible standard—to make their case, they would have to measure and evaluate the content hosted by all online services affected by the law. Both of these cases may be further appealed, and are likely to continue in the lower courts. But people in Georgia and Florida can no longer count on court injunctions to protect their access to the web. What the effects will be going forward depends on how platforms implement these new restrictions, including how they check ages and parental consent, as well as state officials’ views on these efforts. If you hit an age-gate while online, check out our blog post about how you might want to proceed , and our age-gating resource hub . If you want to speak out about your experience, you can talk to us at agegates@eff.org. What is Lost Some youth who lose their social media accounts will lose contact with friends. Others will lose access to a support group, the ability to speak out on current issues, or an audience for their artwork. More young people will be shut out of discussions about what’s going on in their school and their community. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own rights to speak and receive information. These new laws interfere with those rights. The Florida opinion suggests that young people can browse the internet without an account, or use a parent’s account. But that doesn’t help those who might participate in a private group, send a personal message, or speak to an audience they have built up. Nor does it recognize the reality that in many households, young people may not have the ability to use a parent’s device, or even have healthy relationships with their parents. For parents of children under 14, the Florida law also overrides parental autonomy—even if parents wanted to allow their child on these services, they cannot do so by law. These laws won’t just harm younger kids. Adults and older teens will bear the cost of the new rules. In order to figure out who is young enough to not be able to join, or who needs parental consent to join, services will have to check users’ ages. That likely means asking people to submit ID or other sensitive information. Some people will be mis-classified as too young; others will decide that they’d simply rather stop participating instead of handing over even more personal data. Keep A Record Between the recent Meta settlement and these 11th Circuit decisions, despite widespread opposition, age-gating is becoming a reality for the American internet. As these laws are enforced, we need to understand what they mean for the people who have to deal with them. And we need to create a record of their effects on everyone’s speech so we can push to repeal them. If you encounter a restriction due to these laws that affects you, keep a record, ideally while the details are still fresh in your mind. Screenshots, along with notes about the date and time, the service involved, and the task you were trying to accomplish, will all be helpful. Did you lose an account or can’t participate? Describe what you lost. Were you using a group to organize a club, volunteer in your community, or keep in touch with friends? Did losing your account cut you off from people you wouldn’t otherwise be able to be in touch with? Even if you just used the account to access local news or follow your favorite content creator, that’s still a significant loss of your right to access information online. Record problems with age checks and parental consent. What information did the service request from you? Were you able to provide it? Did it reject your age proof, or classify you incorrectly? If you’re a parent, were you able to give permission, and what did you have to provide? What promises did the service make about what it did with the data it collected from you? Save explanations given by the platforms or any services they employ to age gate, including any law they cite. If you are to appeal a result and choose to, keep track of those attempts as well. You can also document choosing to drop out. If you abandon an account or service because you’re unwilling to provide ID or other personal data, write down what you gave up, and why. You don’t need to submit sensitive information to show that you are burdened by new rules. You Can E-Mail agegates@eff.org If these restrictions affect you, we encourage you to reach out to EFF by emailing agegated@eff.org and telling us more about what happened. EFF will continue to oppose laws that prevent adults and minors from expressing themselves online, or that push people to give up their privacy to participate in the digital world. These recent court decisions are setbacks, but they don’t settle the debate. By keeping track of people who lose access, age-check failures, and the online conversations that can no longer happen, we’ll be in a better position to challenge the worst of these restrictions, in both legislatures and courts. And in the meantime, EFF will keep fighting for laws that actually make us safer online—like stopping social media companies’ harmful surveillance of all internet users. We’ll continue to push for laws that empower parents, children, and all internet users to have meaningful choice and control over their online services. Those goals can make everyone safer online, while preserving our ability to speak and access information. Further Action Email EFF about your experience at agegates@eff.org . Uthmeier (Florida) EFF amicus brief in Florida case EFF amicus brief in Georgia case EFF’s Age Verification Hub

title: Canadians Are Running Out Of Time To Oppose The Dangerous C-22 Surveillance Bill
text: Canada’s Parliament is debating a massive expansion of surveillance powers that will threaten the privacy and security of millions of people. Bill C-22, also called the Lawful Access Act, has already passed the House of Commons, and is now before the Canadian Senate. Canadians still have an opportunity to speak out and stop this dangerous legislation. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) is urging all Canadians to sign its petition opposing the bill. (The petition on CCLA’s website is governed by CCLA’s privacy policy.) Take action Tell the canadian senate to stop C-22 As we wrote earlier this year , Bill C-22 gives the government new powers to force digital services—including telecom companies, messaging apps, and more—to help with government surveillance. Worse, it allows Canada’s Minister of Public Safety to order companies to create a backdoor to their services for law enforcement, as long as it doesn’t lead to a “systemic vulnerability.” That’s a clear recipe for weakening the encryption we all rely on. It also requires services to retain metadata for up to a year, which reveals who people communicate with, where they go, and what services they use, even when they are not suspected of any crime. Researchers at CCLA and Citizen Lab published a detailed analysis of C-22 and its serious constitutional and cybersecurity problems. The analysis points out that the bill needs more than cosmetic changes—it calls for entirely withdrawing Part 2 of Bill C-22, the section that establishes the surveillance and data retention regime. Bill C-22 could also expand the sharing of Canadians’ personal data with foreign law enforcement, including the United States. Canada has been negotiating a cross-border data-sharing agreement with the U.S. that would allow American police to get information about Canadian internet users with limited safeguards and oversight. Some Canadian senators have already expressed concerns about the bill, and rightly suggested, as CCLA and Citizen Lab have, that it may not be compatible with privacy protections in the Canadian constitution. If you’re in Canada, read and sign CCLA’s petition opposing Bill C-22 today. Don’t let the Senate allow this dangerous expansion of government surveillance to become Canada’s new reality. Take action Canadians: defend your privacy and security Further reading: Full text of C-22 April: Canadian Civil Liberties Association statement and letter June: CCLA and Citizen Lab researchers release detailed analysis of Bill C-22’s many flaws Open Media blog on C-22 EFF’s analysis of bill C-2

title: An open letter to every family’s designated IT support
text: Almost every family has one. They’re the only ones who know which remote turns on the TV and which controls the volume and channels. They know what an HDMI cable actually does and where to plug it in. They’ve even fixed multiple phone issues within seconds through a little-known, well-kept secret procedure (turning it off and back on). Perhaps they are a parent, tech-savvy sibling, cool aunt or uncle, or close family friend. Whatever the relation, the role stays the same. They are the unpaid, on-call tech specialist for every relative’s forgotten password, printer jam, and device settings update. If this sounds like you, we would first like to thank you for doing a job you never signed up for. Second, we would like to share a simple way you can help your family and friends protect their privacy and security without adding more to your plate. A small settings change that makes a big differenc e With Android and iPhone’s latest releases, and Black Friday deals rapidly approaching, many people are upgrading their current phone to a newer model. As the family’s go-to tech helper, you’ll likely be setting up a few new devices in the near future. You already know the routine: connect to Wi-Fi, choose a language, and transfer data from the old phone to the new one. But beyond the steps you are prompted to take when setting up a new phone lies a quiet decision many people never think twice about: their default browser. While people in some regions, like Europe and Japan, get to choose their default browser when setting up a new phone, this is not the case everywhere . Most phones ship with a browser preinstalled and set as the default, ready to start collecting data and monetizing off user activity the minute it’s opened. title: Five Firefox updates you might have missed, and a look ahead
text: Some of our latest Firefox updates have had big moments of their own, from the launch of our new design and built-in ad blocking on iOS to Firefox Enterprise and our partnership with NVIDIA GeForce NOW . You might’ve even spotted a few familiar internet OGs in our latest campaign . Other improvements might’ve flown under the radar until you open a PDF or move your tabs around. We wanted to take a moment to highlight some of the features and improvements we’ve been working on, from recent additions you might have missed to a look at what’s coming next . What’s new in Firefox Open PDFs faster. Firefox’s built-in PDF viewer now starts up to 45% faster on desktop, so there’s less waiting when you open a document in your browser. Put your Android tabs where you want them. Prefer your tabs at the bottom of the screen? You now have the option to move Firefox’s tab bar there. Go to Settings > Customize to choose. Find your spot in a video faster. We’ve made it quicker to jump to a different point in a video on desktop, whether you’re skipping ahead in a tutorial or going back to catch something you missed. Keep your favorite wallpapers handy. Firefox now saves a collection of your custom wallpapers under “Your images” on New Tab on desktop, so you can switch between favorites without uploading them again. Save time filling out forms and keeping up with page changes. Smart Window can now help fill out online forms using information from your chosen tabs, so you don’t have to copy details back and forth. You can also ask it to watch a page and notify you when something changes, like a price drop or a new job listing, saving you from manually checking for updates. Both capabilities are available in English in the U.S. and Canada as part of the Smart Window beta. Learn more about the new features here . What’s next on the Firefox roadmap When we launched our public roadmap in June, we shared plans to make everyday browsing more useful, flexible and private. We’ve now updated it with more of what’s ahead. We’re developing these features in the open, in close partnership with our contributors, and will share more about release timing as each feature gets ready for more people to try. Here’s a look at what’s in the works: Keep what you need in view. We heard your request for a way to keep a page visible while browsing. Mini Window will let you pop a tab, or part of a page, into a small floating window, so recipes or instructions stay in view while you work in another tab. Listen to pages. Give your eyes a break. Firefox will soon read articles and other web content aloud on desktop and Android, so you can listen while doing other things – even with your phone’s screen off. Take your reading offline. No connection? No problem. Offline mode on Android will let you save articles ahead of time to read or listen to without internet access, perfect for flights and commutes with spotty service. Turn speech into text on desktop. We’re bringing speech recognition to Firefox on desktop, so websites that use Firefox’s built-in capability can offer voice input and captions without sending your audio to a server. Those sites receive the text, while your audio stays on your device. After downloading the speech recognition model, transcription will work offline, too. Choose how VPN works for each site. Since bringing free built-in VPN to Firefox on desktop and Android (iOS coming soon), we’re now adding the ability to set website rules so you can choose how VPN works on a site-by-site basis. Clear browsing data directly from your toolbar. We’re bringing Private Window’s familiar button to Classic Window on desktop, so you can quickly choose what browsing data to delete without digging through settings. Keep shaping Firefox with us Try the latest updates and explore the Firefox roadmap for more of what we’re working on. If there’s something you’re looking forward to, or something you’d like us to improve, tell us on Mozilla Connect . Your feedback helps shape what comes next. The post Five Firefox updates you might have missed, and a look ahead appeared first on The Mozilla Blog .

title: Skip the busywork with Smart Window
text: The days might be getting shorter, but your to-do list is only getting longer. Whether you’re getting a head start on holiday shopping or planning your next career move, Smart Window’s newest features will help you keep up. Firefox’s opt-in AI browsing experience can now use information from tabs you choose to help fill out forms. It can also watch web pages and notify you about specific changes you’ve asked it to track. Let your open tabs fill in the blanks Job applications ask for your work history; event registrations ask for a professional bio. If those details are already in your open tabs, Smart Window can now use pages you choose to suggest what to enter, saving you extra clicks and some Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V. For example, Smart Window could use information from your online portfolio or professional profile to fill in your work history, or draw on those details to draft an answer to a question like “Tell me about a time when…” Firefox’s regular autofill still handles saved information such as your name and address, which can be entered directly into forms without relying on AI models. To get started, click into a form field. If the form has at least four text fields that Smart Window can help fill, you’ll see “Fill from sources” appear in the dropdown, along with a recommended source page. Select “Fill from sources” to continue, or click the pencil icon to open “Edit sources” if you want to change or add tabs. Once you’ve chosen your sources, review the suggestions before filling out the form. You can edit the results before submitting; Smart Window won’t submit the form for you. When you choose to use this feature, information from your selected source pages is shared with Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, the AI model used for detecting the fields and extracting relevant information from your selected tabs. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same, and saved autofill values stay on your device. Learn more about how form filling works . This feature currently supports text fields on web forms and does not save any generated form fill data. We’re exploring support for more field types, including dropdown menus, as well as PDF forms and ways to save and manage generated information for future forms. Give your refresh button a break A watched pot never boils, and refreshing a web page won’t make an update appear any sooner. Smart Window can now watch a page for a specific update, whether that’s an item going on sale or a new job listing that includes a job title or company name that you’re following. Each task can follow up to five pages, so you can keep an eye on several stores or job boards at the same time. Type “/watch” in the Smart Window chat to set up a task. Describe what you’re looking for, add the pages to watch, and choose whether Firefox should check for updates on a daily or weekly basis. Those checks run only while the browser is open. When there’s a match, you’ll see an update through the Tasks button in the toolbar. With desktop notifications enabled, Firefox can also notify you directly; click the notification to open the watched pages. You can have up to 15 active tasks at a time, and you can edit, pause or delete tasks. Smart Window will automatically pause tasks after 60 days without a matching change. If 90 days pass without a change, it will stop checking altogether. Page monitoring uses the Qwen AI model to identify changes that match what you’re looking for. Your model choice for Smart Window chat stays the same. Learn more about creating and managing tasks . Try the latest additions These two new features are available in the Smart Window beta on desktop, in English in the U.S. and Canada, and will roll out to additional markets in the coming months. Try Smart Window and share your experience on Mozilla Connect . We’d love to hear how you’re using Smart Window to get things done and what you’d like it to help with next. title: Firefox reunites meme royalty to remind you what the internet used to feel like
text: A group of familiar faces from the early web just got back together to ask an important question: What happened to the internet? Sure, there was a time when it was a little less polished, and a lot less speedy, but it was yours . Overly Attached Girlfriend may have wanted to know everything about you, but your browser didn’t need to. Dancing Matt boogied all over the world, without any corporations tracking him or selling his personal data. And while Annoying Orange is incredibly annoying, he’s not as annoying as forced AI features. These beloved early internet personalities remind us of a time when surfing the web felt open, organic, and most importantly, personal. And good news: With Firefox, it still can. That’s why we’re teaming up with these icons to remind people what our browser offers, and show those who wandered off why now is the time to come back. The team behind the comeback For Mozilla Chief Marketing Officer John Solomon, the aim of the campaign started with winning back people who originally loved and used Firefox. “I kept going back to Firefox’s heyday, when the internet was really fun, weird, and interesting. The challenge was: how do you lean on nostalgia and heritage, but not be stuck in the past?” The campaign was created by We Believers , one of the world’s most awarded independent agencies, with production handled by nobodys and direction by the Sunny Sixteen collective. “We wanted to create an idea that truly belongs to Firefox — a challenger browser that helped shape the internet’s golden years and stayed independent as Big Tech took over. The goal? Remind former users that what they loved about Firefox matters more than ever now,” said Gustavo Lauria, Founder and CCO at We Believers. Solomon said the finished campaign achieves the goal of embracing Firefox’s history without living in it: “Our partners really cracked it. We wanted to remind people of what made the internet so wonderful in the first place. These are people who helped make it strange, creative, surprising, and fun. None of them were trying to go viral. They were normal, everyday people who were using the internet. That’s the way the internet should be and why we feel it’s a great moment for Firefox. Always independent and unlike big tech, not trying to extract more from everyday people.” The internet you remember is still out there Whether you used Firefox back in the day, or are simply looking for a better browsing experience, we’re still here, staying true to the values we were built on . We believe the internet should be open, accessible, and shaped by the people who use it, not just the platforms that profit from their attention and data. This means a web where you can explore without feeling tracked or used for profit, where you decide for yourself how new technology fits into your life, and you can trust that your browser protects you by default. Firefox has built-in privacy protections to help limit tracking, lets you decide if AI features appear and customize how they behave , and uses open source code that anyone can see . To learn more about what sets Firefox apart, check out five reasons to choose the browser that puts you first . We know a better internet isn’t built by finding new ways to capture your attention or information. It’s about giving you more freedom to make the web your own. The web is yours to explore The internet has changed a lot since Numa Numa Guy first danced his way into our collective memory. But the things that made it magical – creativity, curiosity, community, and the freedom to explore – are still worth protecting. Firefox has championed those values since the beginning, and we’re not giving up on them now. That’s why we’re celebrating the people who helped make the early web what it was, while reminding everyone that a more open, human internet is still an option. The early days of the internet may be behind us, but the spirit doesn’t have to be. Experience it for yourself. Now more than ever: come back to Firefox . title: Still here, still yours: 5 reasons to choose Firefox
text: The internet used to feel like a community, not a commodity. Browsers were tools for exploration, and you could wander the web without feeling tracked everywhere. Today, as the web becomes increasingly surveilled and commercialized, Firefox preserves the magic, freedom, and fun of the early internet. Still open source, still independent, still privacy-focused. No billionaire owner, no hidden agenda. So, whether you’re new here, back after a break, or just curious, here are five reasons to choose the browser that puts you first. Backed by a non-profit, not billionaires Firefox is backed by the Mozilla Foundation, a non-profit committed to an open internet. title: Why is the CMA asking us to choose the furniture before the house? The UK’s search choice screens need browser choice screens alongside them
text: Mobile browsers are a key gateway to the internet for 56 million people in the UK. Smartphone users spend around half an hour a day in these apps, and opening a browser is the most common way they look up information online. Yet most people are using a smartphone browser that was preinstalled and set as the default for them, without ever being asked which browser they would actually prefer. Mozilla believes people deserve an active choice in the tools they depend on every day, which is why the latest proposals from the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) matter. We welcome the CMA’s plans to give people a choice of search service and are asking it to consult on browser choice now, so both screens can launch together. On September 23rd, the CMA published updated plans that would require Google to show people in the UK a choice of search service on new Android devices, covering the default search app and home-screen search widget as well as Chrome. Search choice screens would also appear in Chrome on other platforms, including through a major update for existing users. Some AI assistants would also be eligible to appear alongside search engines. The proposals are well designed, but solve only half the problem The CMA’s mobile browser investigation found that preinstallation, prominent placement and default settings restrict browser competition. Mozilla’s innovative 2023 experiment showed that properly designed browser choice screens can help people choose a browser they expect to keep using, and can be an effective tool for giving people agency over their online life. It also showed that an overwhelming majority of people (98%!) want to see them. The EU Digital Markets Act has since demonstrated their impact in practice. We welcome the CMA’s work on search choice, but people in the UK deserve browser choice too. Asking people to pick a search service inside a browser that most of them never actively chose in the first place leaves some of the biggest issues identified in the CMA’s own mobile browser investigation unaddressed. The CMA commissioned user research on search choice screens to refine and improve the proposals it first consulted on in January. Providers’ positions on the choice screen would be fully randomised. Users would have to scroll to the bottom before confirming, and could “test drive” a search provider for at least a week. The CMA has also recognized that search is changing. Its research found that many people were already using AI assistants to search alongside traditional search services. Under the revised, more technology-neutral eligibility criteria, an AI assistant could also qualify to appear on the search choice screen if it meets the requirements, including being able to search the web and attribute its sources. But browser choice should not be left behind. Why the two choices belong together Less confusion. The CMA’s new research found that participants often confused browsers with search services and were unsure what their search choice would change. Mozilla’s research has revealed similar confusion. These findings support designing and testing the two screens together, with clear explanations of each decision. Less duplication. The CMA’s work on search choice can also inform browser choice. Developing the two together would allow the design, order and timing to be tested as one journey, helping to avoid separate rounds of changes and interruptions for users. Order matters. Nobody chooses the furniture before the house. Browsers have their own search defaults, which is why we recommend showing the browser choice screen first, followed by the search screen, with wording that makes clear these are two separate decisions. The EU and Japan already show both screens The EU’s Digital Markets Act introduced browser choice screens on iOS for the first time and brought browser and search choice together during Android set-up. Browser first, then search, so the relationship between the two makes sense. In Japan, search and browser choice screens are presented on both Android and iOS. And people are making use of the browser screen to select alternatives. In May, we reported Firefox is selected through a DMA choice screen once every ten seconds , with retention five times higher than for organic downloads. Other independent browsers have also reported substantial growth. Choice matters more as AI moves into the browser The CMA’s proposals recognize that AI is changing how people search. AI is also changing what browsers offer, adding to the ways they compete on features, privacy and user control. Firefox already lets people on desktop pick which AI assistant sits in the sidebar , and our Smart Window beta extends that choice to the model behind the browser’s own assistant. There are meaningful differences between browsers. AI is the latest example of why giving people an active choice matters. When people aren’t offered an active browser choice, they may be choosing search and AI services within a browser someone else picked. One decision taken at the factory can end up shaping the ones that follow. A search choice screen gives people a say over their search provider; offering browser choice alongside it would give them a say over that first decision too. Our ask of the CMA We’re asking the CMA to consult now on browser choice screens for Apple’s and Google’s mobile platforms, so they can launch alongside the search screens. Apple and Google already offer browser choice screens in the EU and Japan. The CMA can draw on that experience and its own research to give people in the UK an active choice of both browser and search service. Mozilla’s response to the consultation is available here . We’re asking the CMA to consult now on browser choice screens for Apple’s and Google’s mobile platforms, so they can launch alongside the search screens. title: This map shows the most important asset that VC-backed companies need right now
text: What’s the most vital asset for an AI company today? For venture backed AI business, it might be “funding” or “revenue”. But, there’s another asset that’s just as critical: trust . At Mozilla, building technology that people and businesses can genuinely trust has been a long-standing, guiding principle . That’s why we’re supporting the launch of the Trustworthy AI Map , a market map of VC-backed companies building the infrastructure for trustworthy AI. Supported by seven organizations, including Mozilla, the Trustworthy AI Map features 79 companies across 15 countries, from early to later-stage venture. It maps companies building products for AI deployment across seven layers of the AI stack, including identity, data control, interoperability and evaluation. The map connects the products with the companies and capital behind them, helping investors, founders and businesses explore commercial opportunities. To be featured, trust must be baked into its product or business model through human agency, trust by design or aligned business models. This initiative aligns with much of our work over the past year. We’ve invested in companies through Mozilla Ventures, launched Otari, an open source enterprise tool which allows you to control your LLM infrastructure from a single layer, and published landmark research in our State of Open Source AI report that’s demystifying the open source AI landscape and shows that the capability gap between open and closed models is closing. We’ve also partnered with Mila: the Quebec AI Institute, to build an open source AI foundation layer that enables organizations and institutions to own and operate their own advanced AI systems locally, ensuring full control over their technology and data. The project has the backing of the Canadian government, and industry leaders like Hypertec. At a time when fear and uncertainty about AI are on the rise, trust is not just a virtue; it’s a path towards profitability. Explore the Trustworthy AI Map to see how. Learn more at trustworthyaimap.org . The post This map shows the most important asset that VC-backed companies need right now appeared first on The Mozilla Blog .

title: What does the (Fire)fox say?
text: It all started with a question: What does Firefox sound like to you? Over the past year, Mozilla developed a small but meaningful set of sounds to add a sonic dimension to the Firefox experience. When we started this process, we knew we wanted something warm, human, and representative of our open source identity. We also knew we didn’t want to invent these sounds in a vacuum. So we did what we’ve always done and turned to our community. With the help of creative audio company Sounds Like These , we reached out to Firefox users, contributors, and team members across the globe asking them to send us audio and written descriptions of what Firefox sounds like to them. This feedback became our compass. From there, we began building three new sounds that bring to life our logo, mascot Kit , and Firefox notifications. The logo and Kit sound have already begun rolling out across the Firefox brand (check them out in our new design launch announcement ) – and we’re excited to bring the notification sound to the browser in a future update. Not only did we want these new sounds to reflect Mozilla’s mission and values, we also wanted to ensure they felt connected to one another. This is the story of how they came to be. The logo sound: A human chorus rooted in nature Because Mozilla uses a community-based approach to create world-class open source software, we wanted Firefox’s audio logo to share this same spirit. This meant creating something built by many and rooted in real human experience. Inspired by early community feedback that associated Firefox with nature, we started with delicate organic textures, including bird song and the thump of wood being struck to evoke the feeling of Kit moving through different environments. We also knew we wanted to utilize the voices of real Mozilla employees, or “Mozillians.” As Sounds Like These Co-founder Sam Heath reflected, “What better way to represent the brand than the sound of the people behind it?” At first, we considered setting up a professional recording session in a large city where multiple Mozillians could drop in to be recorded. However, we quickly realized this would limit the voices we would be able to include to one geographic location. It was then suggested: Why not just let people record wherever they are? After all, Firefox is used in family living rooms, shared offices, and really most places one can access the internet. The final result includes the voices of 23 real Mozillians saying “Firefox!”, in which you can hear their subtle differences in accent, tone, and timing. Sam shared that some of these employee submissions included the echoes of distant chatter, families, and all the other subtle sounds of Mozillians’ real life playing out as they recorded. He explained that Sounds Like These did not deliberately edit out the entirety of this ambient sound to preserve the texture and authenticity that comes from real people living their real lives. “That was something that was very clear from Mozilla from the start. We don’t want to be this shiny, distracting tech brand. We wanted this to feel real, natural, and human,” said Sam. The Kit sound: Friendly, familiar, and uniquely Firefox Kit holds the prestigious title of VP of Mascoting at Firefox, and we worked hard to ensure their sound properly reflects such an important position. Kit’s not an AI assistant, nor a chatbot. They’re not an actual fox, or a red panda either. They’re a Firefox, its own creature not of this world. Kit may appear in your Firefox browser during moments that are meant to feel welcoming and encouraging, like when you’re getting started, trying out a new feature, or successfully making a settings change. Our goal when creating the Kit sound was to convey Kit’s friendly, familiar, and trustworthy presence without mimicking any real animal. The sound had to be flexible enough to express movement and emotion across animations and videos, while also remaining instantly recognizable. Early experiments ranged from pure animal sounds to abstract musical expressions. Foxes were considered, but as Sam noted, “Foxes are incredibly difficult to record, and they do make cute sounds, but never around people. You only really seem to hear them literally screaming – and we definitely didn’t want anyone screaming.” We also explored a more feline route, specifically a cat purr. As Oli Slack, Co-Founder and Head of Audio at Sounds Like These, explains, “The cat purr was almost kind of perfect…other than the fact that it sounded just like a cat purring. So we asked, ‘How do we recreate the feeling of what the purr sounds like, without it being an actual cat purr?’” This is where the process really got interesting. While brainstorming cat purr alternatives, the Sounds Like These team researched the psychology behind what makes certain sounds more comforting and familiar. Soft tones and warmth from other humans instinctively register as more reassuring and honest, and this also crosses over into animals, particularly animals we keep as companions. This validated our initial draw toward the cat purr, and confirmed we were heading in the right direction sonically. The breakthrough came when Sounds Like These stopped looking at animal sounds as a starting point, instead using a human voice as the basis of a custom purr. This wasn’t someone imitating a cat or “purring” themselves, it served as a foundation vocalization that was then uniquely shaped and layered to convey Kit’s friendly and encouraging presence. And thus, the Kit sound was born. The notification sound: A gentle whoosh of helpfulness, coming soon to Firefox Notifications don’t have to be jarring or intrusive, and that’s exactly what we wanted to avoid when creating one for Firefox. Our new notification sound – which we look forward to rolling out in a future Firefox update – was carefully crafted to gently alert, not interrupt. It draws inspiration from community feedback that described the feeling of using Firefox like a door opening and referenced moments of quiet discovery filled with gentle wonderment and joy. This sense of seamless exploration is reflected in the sound’s design: a soft whoosh, like a door swinging open, followed by a subtle click, all in an airy, rounded tone to feel helpful, not demanding. The result is a sound that softly notifies rather than disrupts or controls, staying true to the feeling of joyful curiosity that many users associate with browsing the web through Firefox. A family of sounds shaped by community From the very beginning of this process, we leaned into Mozilla’s values of openness and community. We consulted our fans and team members. We used real voices. We embraced the imperfections of being human. These sounds are now a part of Firefox’s story, and we hope every time you hear them, they remind you that you’re using a browser built by the people, for the people. title: Jambu Palaniappan and David Parry-Jones join the Mozilla Corporation Board of Directors
text: Today, we are very pleased to announce two new additions to the Mozilla Corporation Board of Directors: Jambu Palaniappan and David Parry-Jones. As we build the next chapter of Mozilla, we’ve been focused on bringing people onto our Board who combine deep operating experience with a real commitment to the values Mozilla stands for. Jambu and David bring deep experience building and leading technology businesses, and each brings a unique perspective to our Board. Jambu Palaniappan is the Chief Executive Officer of Checkatrade, where he drives the company’s mission of Powering Great Work. The home improvement platform connects consumers across the UK with quality tradespeople — every year, Checkatrade improves millions of homes and delivers billions of pounds of work to small and medium-sized businesses. Before joining Checkatrade, Jambu was Managing Partner and Head of Europe at OMERS Ventures, where he invested in and supported high-growth technology companies. Earlier in his career, he spent several years at Uber and Uber Eats, joining as one of the first 100 employees and leading expansion across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Jambu holds a degree in Public Policy and Economics from Vanderbilt University. David Parry-Jones is a board director and former Chief Revenue Officer (CRO) with more than 30 years of experience scaling technology businesses internationally. Most recently, he served as CRO at DeepL and previously held senior leadership roles at Microsoft, VMware, and Twilio. He has led large teams across diverse markets and cultures, working with both early-stage companies and global enterprises. As a board member and adviser, he brings a practical perspective on growth, international expansion, and building strong teams that turn strategy into results. Please join me in welcoming Jambu and David to the Mozilla Corporation Board of Directors. title: 100 days later: Microsoft still steers Windows and Copilot users to Edge, everywhere the law lets it
text: One hundred days ago, Mozilla released Over The Edge 2.0, the second independent report from leading experts on deceptive design Dr. Harry Brignull and Cennydd Bowles, on how Windows, Edge, Bing, and Copilot are designed to steer people away from the browser they chose. We published the report , and the researchers published the evidence for anyone to analyze. Browsers are a powerful tool. So it’s no surprise that the history of the web has many examples of powerful platforms trying to deny people browser choice. Now, as AI reshapes our online experiences, the stakes couldn’t be higher. Browsers are a key distribution layer for AI tools and services, while still determining many of the privacy and security functionality people rely on every day. Steering people toward one browser can therefore shape which AI services reach users and the protections that come with it. We also shared the report with Microsoft and talked to them about the issues raised in the report. We knew that an immediate change was unlikely, but we hoped that, when faced with independent evidence of harmful design practices impacting Windows users, they would also want better for people. Instead, it became clear that Microsoft will respect user choice only when it is forced to. It is important to think about what that means for a company whose operating system runs on more than a billion machines. Microsoft’s standard for respecting people’s choices is legal compliance. Not what’s best for its users. Not its own published principles. Not what’s technically feasible. Not even what it already does for users in Europe. That’s the most shocking part. Not that Microsoft engages in such tactics – we’ve seen that before. It’s the fact that a better version of Windows already exists, and it is already available today – but only if you live in the European Economic Area (EEA), where the Digital Markets Act (DMA) forced the issue. If you live in the United States, India, the United Kingdom, or most other locations around the world, your experience and your freedom to choose for yourself are worse. One hundred days later, here is what people outside of the EEA still get: The Windows 10 message “You’re almost done setting up your PC” uses tricky wording to pull people off the default they picked. Windows Search and Widgets open links in Edge instead of the browser set as default. Windows keeps Edge as the default for common browser file types like PDFs and SVG images, even after another browser has been set as default. And people in the EEA also deserve better: Edge remains pre-pinned to the taskbar; this seems to directly violate the “principled approach to app pinning and app defaults.” Copilot, Microsoft’s AI tool opens web links in a side-panel instead of the browser people chose, in every region tested, Europe included. Windows Backup, the tool Microsoft uses to guide people through the migration to Windows 11, silently tries to set Edge as the default when it restores a PC and fails to properly bring the user’s own browser along. Most of the 2024 patterns are still there. The 2026 patterns are worse. Microsoft is using new surfaces like Copilot and the migration to Windows 11 to further undermine user choice. Our ask has always been simple: First, give all Windows users the fairer designs that are live in the EEA – regardless of where they are located. Second, stop the remaining harmful design practices that persist in the EEA. That means: Stopping the remaining harmful design tactics in the EEA and ship that standard worldwide. Honoring people’s browser choice everywhere it is currently ignored, including Windows Search, Widgets, Copilot, and Windows Backup restoration. Applying Microsoft’s own 2023 app pinning principles to Edge itself. The Mozilla-commissioned report has never been about intent. It’s about accountability and Microsoft’s responsibility to stop undermining people’s choices. The practices we documented need to change. Statements about intent are not a substitute for action. In the past 100 days, we’ve stopped waiting for Microsoft to act. Instead, we’ve stepped up public pressure on the company to respect people’s choices. We are also taking the report’s findings to regulators and policymakers. In Europe, the DMA is the only thing that has moved Microsoft. Everywhere else, the lesson is the same: Microsoft ships only when a regulator requires fairer design. We hope that regulators in the US, the UK, India, and Brazil are paying attention. Microsoft can do better. It already has, for people in the EEA. Until it does the same in all jurisdictions, we will keep pointing out the company’s choices and the impact they have on hundreds of millions of users who want something different. Browsers are a powerful tool. So it’s no surprise that the history of the web has many examples of powerful platforms trying to deny people browser choice. Now, as AI reshapes our online experiences, the stakes couldn’t be higher. Browsers are a key distribution layer for AI tools and services, while still determining many of the privacy and security functionality people rely on every day. Steering people toward one browser can therefore shape which AI services reach users and the protections that come with it. 

We also shared the report with Microsoft and talked to them about the issues raised in the report. We knew that an immediate change was unlikely, but we hoped that, when faced with independent evidence of harmful design practices impacting Windows users, they would also want better for people.

Instead, it became clear that Microsoft will respect user choice only when it is forced to. It is important to think about what that means for a company whose operating system runs on more than a billion machines. Microsoft’s standard for respecting people’s choices is legal compliance. Not what’s best for its users. Not its own published principles. Not what’s technically feasible. Not even what it already does for users in Europe.

That’s the most shocking part. Not that Microsoft engages in such tactics – we’ve seen that before. It’s the fact that a better version of Windows already exists, and it is already available today – but only if you live in the European Economic Area (EEA), where the Digital Markets Act (DMA) forced the issue. If you live in the United States, India, the United Kingdom, or most other locations around the world, your experience and your freedom to choose for yourself are worse.

One hundred days later, here is what people outside of the EEA still get: 

  • The Windows 10 message “You’re almost done setting up your PC” uses tricky wording to pull people off the default they picked. 
  • Windows Search and Widgets open links in Edge instead of the browser set as default. 
  • Windows keeps Edge as the default for common browser file types like PDFs and SVG images, even after another browser has been set as default.

And people in the EEA also deserve better:

  • Edge remains pre-pinned to the taskbar; this seems to directly violate the “principled approach to app pinning and app defaults.” 
  • Copilot, Microsoft’s AI tool opens web links in a side-panel instead of the browser people chose, in every region tested, Europe included.
  • Windows Backup, the tool Microsoft uses to guide people through the migration to Windows 11, silently tries to set Edge as the default when it restores a PC and fails to properly bring the user’s own browser along. 

Most of the 2024 patterns are still there. The 2026 patterns are worse. Microsoft is using new surfaces like Copilot and the migration to Windows 11 to further undermine user choice.

Our ask has always been simple: First, give all Windows users the fairer designs that are live in the EEA – regardless of where they are located. Second, stop the remaining harmful design practices that persist in the EEA. That means:

  • Stopping the remaining harmful design tactics in the EEA and ship that standard worldwide.
  • Honoring people’s browser choice everywhere it is currently ignored, including Windows Search, Widgets, Copilot, and Windows Backup restoration. 
  • Applying Microsoft’s own 2023 app pinning principles to Edge itself. 

The Mozilla-commissioned report has never been about intent. It’s about accountability and Microsoft’s responsibility to stop undermining people’s choices. The practices we documented need to change. Statements about intent are not a substitute for action.

In the past 100 days, we’ve stopped waiting for Microsoft to act. Instead, we’ve stepped up public pressure on the company to respect people’s choices.

We are also taking the report’s findings to regulators and policymakers. In Europe, the DMA is the only thing that has moved Microsoft. Everywhere else, the lesson is the same: Microsoft ships only when a regulator requires fairer design. 

We hope that regulators in the US, the UK, India, and Brazil are paying attention. 

Microsoft can do better. It already has, for people in the EEA.

Until it does the same in all jurisdictions, we will keep pointing out the company’s choices and the impact they have on hundreds of millions of users who want something different.

title: Strengthen your online security for free with Firefox
text: Every October, Cybersecurity Awareness Month reminds us the importance of protecting our digital lives. The theme for 2026 is ‘ Don’t Make It Easy for Them, ’ with the National Cybersecurity Alliance (NCA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) providing simple, actionable steps users can take to make it harder for cybercriminals to attack. Everyone wants to be safe online, but one of the most common excuses we hear is “I don’t have the time or the money to invest in it right now.” Well, we have good news: you can improve your online security easily, for the low price of $0. Firefox provides several free features designed to make it easier to protect your online life and harder for cybercriminals to target you. Password manager: Use a unique password for every account Reused passwords are one of the easiest ways attackers break into multiple accounts. If one site is breached, your login details could be tested on many others. Firefox’s free password manager can generate and securely store a strong, unique password per site, which is the single highest-leverage fix against password stuffing. For convenience, Firefox can automatically fill in your saved login information the next time you access a previously visited site. However, you still have the option to turn off password saving for specific websites, or completely if you’re using a shared device or simply prefer to enter it each time. You can manage your stored logins on a singular device at any time. To get a head start, you also have the option to import passwords saved on several other popular browsers. In addition, you can create a free Mozilla account to safely sync them across your signed-in devices. VPN: Privacy built into the browser Imagine you’re settling into a corner table at a bustling airport cafe, checking some emails on your phone before you board your flight. Or perhaps you took your laptop to the campus library to finally start that research paper you’ve been putting off. Maybe you’re polishing off that last presentation slide between sessions at an out-of-state conference. While these moments are routine, connecting to public Wi-Fi anywhere can open a small window of risk – as your IP address, approximate location, and browsing activity can be more exposed on networks you don’t control. That’s where Firefox’s free built-in, browser-based VPN steps in. While Firefox already encrypts your traffic with HTTPS, the built-in VPN feature routes your browsing traffic through a proxy network, hiding your IP address before it reaches a website. This means the sites you visit will see a proxy IP address instead of your own. It offers an industry-leading 50 gigabytes of free VPN-browsing each month, with no extension or extra app to install. Simply sign in, turn it on, and start browsing. Firefox’s free built-in VPN first launched on desktop in March, later expanding to Android in July. Unlike a standalone or full-service VPN, it’s designed specifically to protect your browsing traffic within Firefox, not your entire device. This means apps, downloads, and other system traffic are not routed through the browser-based VPN. For people who need broader, device-wide VPN protection, Mozilla also offers a separate paid VPN service . You can check the full list of regions where built-in VPN in Firefox is currently available here , and learn more about the differences between Firefox’s free built-in VPN and Mozilla VPN here . Relay: Contain the damage of any one breach Think about how often you give out your personal email address – for an online purchase, RSVPing to an event, or signing up to a new app. Each time, you trust the site owner will protect your information, but, spam piles up and breaches can still happen – even when you think you’re being careful. Firefox Relay gives you a smarter way to share. Instead of handing out your real email address, this feature provides secure, random email masks to use any time a website, store, or app asks you for your information. It forwards messages to your real email, while keeping your identity hidden to senders. This means if one service gets compromised, your other accounts stay safe. You can also use Relay in the U.S. and Canada to shield your phone number , so you can receive calls and texts through masks and reply without exposing your real number. The best part? To make protecting your privacy even easier, Firefox increased its limit to 50 free email masks earlier this year, allowing you to shield dozens of logins at no cost. Browse freely: Firefox protects you by default Even if you sometimes forget to use Firefox protection tools like password manager, VPN, and Relay, there are multiple always-on features operating within the browser to help keep your session secure and private. These include enhanced tracking protection to block hidden scripts and known trackers that follow you across the web, browser fingerprinting protection to prevent sites from building a unique profile of your device, and warnings about deceptive or malicious websites. Together, Firefox’s individual and always-on security features work to help keep your browsing safe and your data private. So, this Cybersecurity Awareness Month, take a moment to build new habits, try out our free cybersecurity tools, and make life more difficult for cybercriminals. Small steps add up, and we are here to help. Stay safe, stay smart, and keep exploring the web with confidence on Firefox. title: Under the Hood: Prompt tuning Shake to Summarize for recipes
text: Following the rollout of Firefox’s Shake to Summarize feature to Android devices this May, we wanted to take a closer look at the modeling work behind the feature. In a previous blog post , we discussed our model selection process. Now that Shake to Summarize has been available on both iOS and Android for a few months, we wanted to take it a step further and outline our approach to prompt development. This is the story of a Shake to Summarize use case that required a little extra prompt tuning: online recipes. Framing the Problem The first step in developing a useful prompt is clearly describing what you want the LLM to do. LLMs thrive on specificity, so the more sharply you can define your task, the better your results are likely to be. This is especially important when using smaller LLMs (like we are here), since these little models are not as good at reading between the lines and intuiting unstated intentions as their more powerful cousins are. If the recipe says “cook lovingly” we might be OK with shortening it to “cook,” but if it calls for 4 cups of vegetable broth, a Tbsp of oregano and a tsp of thyme, we want these details relayed to us exactly . Merely stating, “this recipe calls for some broth and some spices” would not be adequate.
